cities.quote: What a wonder it is! So grand, so solemn, so vast! And yet so delicate, so airy, so graceful!
cities.heroTitle: Milan hero — Steffen Schmitz (CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons)
cities.preamble:
- Milan speaks standard Italian with a northern accent. The old Milanese dialect survives mostly among older people and in a handful of phrases everyone knows.
- An *s* between vowels is buzzed like a z here: *casa* sounds like “kaza.” Every letter is still pronounced, and double consonants are held longer.
- English is common in the centre, in business and fashion, and in hotels. Milan is Italy’s working city and moves quickly, so keep exchanges short and polite.
- Greet people entering a shop or bar, and again on the way out. Coffee is drunk standing at the counter, and fast.

cities.quote: What are you doing here, poet, on the ruins of St. John’s Cathedral this sunny day in spring? What are you thinking here, where the wind blowing from the Vistula scatters the red dust of the rubble?
cities.heroTitle: Warsaw hero — Rhododendrites (CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons)
cities.preamble:
- Warsaw speaks standard Polish, with little regional accent, and more English than anywhere else in Poland, especially among people under forty.
- Use pan (sir) and pani (madam) with strangers and people behind counters. The informal form is for friends and people your age.
- Greet people in shops with dzień dobry and say do widzenia leaving. Skipping it reads as rude.
- *sz* is “sh,” *cz* is “ch,” *w* is “v,” *ł* is “w,” and *rz* sounds like the s in “pleasure.” Stress almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable.

cities.quote: I was born in Belfast between the mountain and the gantries / To the hooting of lost sirens and the clang of trams
cities.heroTitle: Belfast hero — Simon Burchell (CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons)
cities.preamble:
- English, with an Ulster accent that runs fast and moves its vowels around. Irish and Ulster Scots turn up on some signs; neither is widely spoken day to day.
- Belfast is friendly and direct, and strangers will talk to you at bus stops. The humour is dry and teasing, and being slagged off by a new friend is a good sign.
- Words carry sides here. Place names, flags, football shirts and Derry versus Londonderry all signal something, so follow how the person you’re talking to says it.
- Prices are in pounds sterling. Northern Irish banks print their own notes, which look unfamiliar but spend the same.

cities.quote: Liverpool is the “pool of life.” The “liver,” according to an old view, is the seat of life — that which “makes to live.”
cities.heroTitle: Liverpool hero — The Carlisle Kid (CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons)
cities.preamble:
- English, spoken with Scouse, the fast, sing-song Liverpool accent shaped by Irish and Welsh migrants and the port. It sounds nothing like Manchester, 30 miles away, and locals would rather you didn’t compare them.
- Liverpool talks. Strangers chat at bus stops and bars, and teasing is friendly. A quick reply goes down better than a polite one.
- The city is red or blue: Liverpool FC or Everton. Families split down the middle, and someone will ask which you support.
- Many shops won’t sell *The Sun* newspaper, over its false 1989 coverage of the Hillsborough disaster, a stadium crush in which 97 Liverpool fans died. It is not a subject for jokes.

cities.quote: “Glasgow is a magnificent city,” said McAlpin. “Why do we hardly ever notice that?” “Because nobody imagines living here,” said Thaw.
cities.attr: Alasdair Gray, novelist and artist, Lanark (1981)
cities.heroTitle: Glasgow hero — Michael D Beckwith (CC0, Wikimedia Commons)
cities.preamble:
- English, with a Glasgow accent and a set of Scots words that visitors from England find harder than Edinburgh’s. People will slow down if you ask.
- Glasgow is famously open. Strangers start conversations at bus stops and in pub queues, and a short answer reads as unfriendly rather than polite.
- The humour is dry, quick and often at someone’s expense, including yours. Giving some back is expected.
- Football runs deep. Celtic and Rangers are a divide with religious and political history, so don’t pick a side casually or wear either strip into a pub.

storyTitle.en-US: Confessions

storyDescription.en-US: Augustine’s account of his own life, written around 400. The turning point comes in Milan: a crisis in a garden in 386, then baptism by the city’s bishop, Ambrose, at Easter 387. Ambrose lies in the crypt of Sant’Ambrogio, the brick church he founded.

storyTitle.en-US: Leonardo and the Last Supper

storyDescription.en-US: Art historian Ross King on how Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper in the 1490s for Duke Ludovico Sforza, while war closed in on Milan. It is short and clear. The mural is still on the dining-hall wall of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent.

storyTitle.en-US: The Betrothed

storyDescription.en-US: Italy’s great 19th-century novel: two village lovers kept apart by a local lord, with bread riots and the plague of 1630 in Milan. It’s long. Alessandro Manzoni lived and died in the house on Via Morone, now a museum of his life.

locationName.en-US: Casa del Manzoni museum, Via Morone

storyTitle.en-US: Calcio: A History of Italian Football

storyDescription.en-US: Historian John Foot on Italian football: the clubs, the fans, the scandals and the money. Milan has two of the biggest clubs, AC Milan and Inter. They share one ground, the San Siro stadium, which opened in 1926 and holds about 75,000.

storyTitle.en-US: The Body of Il Duce

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Sergio Luzzatto follows Benito Mussolini’s corpse after partisans shot him in April 1945. It was hung upside down from a petrol station roof on Piazzale Loreto, now a busy traffic square, then buried, stolen and fought over for years.

storyTitle.en-US: Poem Strip

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist Dino Buzzati retold the Orpheus myth as a comic book set in 1960s Milan: a pop singer follows his dead lover through a door in a city street into the afterlife. Buzzati spent his working life at the Corriere della Sera newspaper on Via Solferino.

locationName.en-US: Corriere della Sera offices, Via Solferino

storyTitle.en-US: Accidental Death of an Anarchist

storyDescription.en-US: A farce by Nobel-winning playwright Dario Fo. In December 1969 anarchist Giuseppe Pinelli fell to his death from a window of Milan’s police headquarters, held after the Piazza Fontana bank bombing that killed 17. Fo mocks the official story.

storyTitle.en-US: The Sack of Rome

storyDescription.en-US: Journalist Alexander Stille on Silvio Berlusconi, the Milan builder who made a TV fortune, owned AC Milan and became prime minister. It covers the 1990s Clean Hands bribery inquiry, run from the Palace of Justice, the city’s vast 1930s courthouse.

storyTitle.en-US: The House of Gucci

storyDescription.en-US: Fashion journalist Sara Gay Forden on how a Florentine leather firm became a global brand and a family war. In 1995 Maurizio Gucci was shot dead on the steps of his office at Via Palestro 20. His ex-wife, Patrizia Reggiani, was convicted of ordering it.

storyTitle.en-US: Italian Ways: On and Off the Rails from Milan to Palermo

storyDescription.en-US: English novelist Tim Parks, who has taught in Milan for years, reads Italy through its trains: ticket rules, commuters, strikes and the new fast lines. Much of it starts at Milano Centrale, the vast stone station finished under Mussolini in 1931.

storyTitle.en-US: Miracle in Milan

storyDescription.en-US: Original title Miracolo a Milano. Vittorio De Sica’s postwar fable, written with Cesare Zavattini: a kind orphan leads a shantytown against a greedy landowner. It ends with the poor flying on broomsticks over Piazza del Duomo, the cathedral square.

storyTitle.en-US: Maria by Callas

storyDescription.en-US: Tom Volf’s documentary tells soprano Maria Callas’s life in her own words, from interviews, letters and home movies. La Scala, Milan’s opera house, was the centre of her career in the 1950s, when she and director Luchino Visconti staged operas there.

storyTitle.en-US: Rocco and His Brothers

storyDescription.en-US: Luchino Visconti’s drama about a widow and her five sons who move from the poor south to Milan during the 1950s boom. It runs nearly three hours. Its darkest scene was shot on the shore of the Idroscalo, a rowing lake by Linate airport.

storyTitle.en-US: La Notte

storyDescription.en-US: Michelangelo Antonioni follows a novelist (Marcello Mastroianni) and his wife (Jeanne Moreau) through a day and night as their marriage runs down. It opens on the glass face of Gio Ponti’s new Pirelli Tower skyscraper. It is slow by design.

storyTitle.en-US: Teorema

storyDescription.en-US: Pier Paolo Pasolini’s allegory: a mysterious young guest (Terence Stamp) upends each member of a rich Milan factory owner’s family. The owner hands his factory to the workers and ends up stripping naked in Milano Centrale, the main railway station.

storyTitle.en-US: Piazza Fontana: The Italian Conspiracy

storyDescription.en-US: Original title Romanzo di una strage. Marco Tullio Giordana on the 12 December 1969 bombing of an agricultural bank on Piazza Fontana, a square behind the Duomo, which killed 17. The courts later blamed a neo-fascist cell. No one was punished.

locationName.en-US: Piazza Fontana, site of the agricultural bank

storyTitle.en-US: House of Gucci

storyDescription.en-US: Ridley Scott’s drama from Sara Gay Forden’s book, with Lady Gaga as Patrizia Reggiani and Adam Driver as Maurizio Gucci, whom she had killed in 1995. He was shot on the steps of his office at Via Palestro 20, a street along the public gardens.

storyTitle.en-US: I Am Love

storyDescription.en-US: Original title Io sono l’amore. Luca Guadagnino’s drama about a rich Milan textile family, with Tilda Swinton as the Russian-born wife who falls for a young chef. The family home is Villa Necchi Campiglio, a 1930s villa now run as a house museum.

storyTitle.en-US: Il Posto

storyDescription.en-US: Original title means “the job.” Ermanno Olmi’s quiet drama about a shy teenager from the town of Meda who commutes into Milan, sits the entrance tests for a big company and finds a dead-end desk. Trains from Meda end at Cadorna station.

Sky series created by actor Stefano Accorsi, set during Mani Pulite (“clean hands”), the 1992 bribery inquiry by Milan magistrates that brought down Italy’s main parties. The investigators worked from the city’s Palace of Justice.

storyTitle.en-US: Mitridate, re di Ponto, K. 87: Overture

storyDescription.en-US: Mozart was 14 when his first opera seria, “Mithridates, King of Pontus,” opened on 26 December 1770 at the Teatro Regio Ducale, the court theatre in the Palazzo Reale palace beside the Duomo. That theatre burned in 1776; La Scala replaced it.

storyTitle.en-US: L’elisir d’amore: Una furtiva lagrima

storyDescription.en-US: Donizetti’s comic opera “The Elixir of Love” premiered in 1832 at the Teatro della Canobbiana, now the Teatro Lirico on Via Larga. This tenor aria, “A furtive tear,” is its best-known number. The theatre was renamed for singer Giorgio Gaber in 2021.

storyTitle.en-US: Nabucco: Va, pensiero

storyDescription.en-US: The Hebrew slaves’ chorus, “Go, thought, on golden wings,” made Verdi’s name at La Scala in 1842. When his body was moved in 1901 to the rest home for musicians he founded, Casa Verdi on Piazza Buonarroti, crowds sang it. He lies in its crypt.

locationName.en-US: Casa Verdi rest home, Piazza Buonarroti

storyTitle.en-US: Messa da Requiem: Dies irae

storyDescription.en-US: Verdi wrote his Requiem to honour novelist Alessandro Manzoni, author of “The Betrothed,” and conducted the first performance on 22 May 1874 in San Marco church in Brera, a year after Manzoni’s death. “Dies irae” means “day of wrath.”

storyTitle.en-US: Madama Butterfly: Un bel dì vedremo

storyDescription.en-US: Puccini’s “Madama Butterfly” was booed at its La Scala premiere on 17 February 1904. He withdrew it, revised it, and it triumphed in Brescia months later. In Cio-Cio-San’s aria, “One fine day we’ll see,” she hopes that her American husband returns.

storyTitle.en-US: O mia bela Madunina

storyDescription.en-US: Songwriter Giovanni D’Anzi’s dialect anthem, “Oh my beautiful little Madonna,” salutes the gilded Virgin on the highest spire of the Duomo cathedral, a Milanese symbol since 1774. Fans still sing it at the San Siro stadium.

storyTitle.en-US: Ma mi

storyDescription.en-US: Theatre director Giorgio Strehler wrote these dialect words, “But me,” for singer Ornella Vanoni (1934–2025): a resistance prisoner held in San Vittore prison who refuses to name names. It belongs to her “canzoni della mala,” songs of the Milan underworld.

storyTitle.en-US: Porta Romana

storyDescription.en-US: Milanese singer and theatre-maker Giorgio Gaber (1939–2003) sings of the working-class streets and bars around Porta Romana, the 1596 stone gate on the old Spanish walls where the road to Rome left the city.

storyTitle.en-US: Il ragazzo della via Gluck

storyDescription.en-US: Adriano Celentano grew up at No. 14 on Via Gluck, behind the Central Station. “The boy from Via Gluck” mourns the fields there lost to postwar concrete, an early Italian protest song about urban sprawl, sung at the 1966 Sanremo festival.

storyTitle.en-US: Vengo anch’io. No, tu no

storyDescription.en-US: Doctor, songwriter and comic Enzo Jannacci (1935–2013) had his biggest hit with this absurdist refrain, “I’m coming too. No, not you.” He was a pillar of the Derby Club on Viale Monte Rosa, the cabaret where Milan’s satirical comedy scene grew up.

locationName.en-US: Derby Club site, Viale Monte Rosa

storyTitle.en-US: Luci a San Siro

storyDescription.en-US: Songwriter Roberto Vecchioni remembers courting by car in the dark near the San Siro stadium: “Lights at San Siro,” with the floodlights of Inter and AC Milan’s shared ground as the backdrop. It became one of the best-loved Milan songs.

storyTitle.en-US: Badabum Cha Cha

storyDescription.en-US: Rapper Marracash, born Fabio Bartolo Rizzo to Sicilian parents, grew up in the Barona housing estates on Milan’s southwest edge. This lead single from his 2008 debut album helped take Milan street rap into the Italian charts.

storyTitle.en-US: Tran Tran

storyDescription.en-US: Sfera Ebbasta, real name Gionata Boschetti, comes from Cinisello Balsamo, a commuter town just north of Milan, and built Italian trap there with producer Charlie Charles. The title is slang for the daily grind; the town square is Piazza Gramsci.

storyTitle.en-US: Cara Italia

storyDescription.en-US: Ghali Amdouni, son of Tunisian parents, grew up in Baggio on Milan’s western outskirts. “Dear Italy” is a love letter to the country that questions who counts as Italian, from a rapper born and raised in Milan.

storyTitle.en-US: Soldi

storyDescription.en-US: Singer Mahmood, Sardinian mother and Egyptian father, grew up in Gratosoglio, the high-rise estate on Milan’s southern edge. “Money” is about a father who left, with an Arabic line; it won Sanremo in 2019 and came second at Eurovision.

storyTitle.en-US: A blacksmith’s son founds Fascism in a Milan hall

storyDescription.en-US: Paul McGann narrates the rise of Benito Mussolini, the socialist editor turned dictator. In March 1919 he founded the Fasci di Combattimento, the first Fascist movement, at a meeting in a hall on Piazza San Sepolcro, a small square near the Duomo.

storyTitle.en-US: Young Fascists dig up Mussolini’s body and hide it for months

storyDescription.en-US: Mussolini was buried in an unmarked grave in Milan’s Cimitero Maggiore cemetery. In April 1946 neo-Fascist Domenico Leccisi and friends dug him up and hid the body; it was recovered and later reburied in his home town, Predappio.

storyTitle.en-US: Milan’s bishop bargains with a usurper

storyDescription.en-US: Mike Duncan’s The History of Rome reaches 383, when Milan was an imperial capital and its new bishop, Ambrose, helped negotiate a power-sharing deal with the rebel general Magnus Maximus. Ambrose lies in the crypt of the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio.

storyTitle.en-US: A family of lords tightens its grip on the city

storyDescription.en-US: When Azzone Visconti died in 1339, his uncles Luchino and Giovanni took over Milan and kept expanding it, ending the old self-governing commune. Azzone’s marble tomb is in San Gottardo in Corte, the church of his palace behind the Royal Palace.

storyTitle.en-US: A mercenary becomes duke and builds a hospital for the poor

storyDescription.en-US: Mark Rasmussen follows Francesco Sforza, the mercenary captain who became Duke of Milan in 1450, and his dissolute son Galeazzo Maria. Francesco founded the Ospedale Maggiore, the vast hospital now called Ca’ Granda and used by the University of Milan.

locationName.en-US: Ca’ Granda, the former Ospedale Maggiore

storyTitle.en-US: Leonardo paints a castle hall into a forest

storyDescription.en-US: Leonardo da Vinci spent most of his early career serving Ludovico Sforza, “il Moro,” regent and then Duke of Milan. In the Castello Sforzesco, the ducal castle, he painted the Sala delle Asse as an arbour of interlaced mulberry branches.

storyTitle.en-US: An opera house named after the church it replaced

storyDescription.en-US: Holly Frey and Tracy V. Wilson’s 2014 episode on the Teatro alla Scala, opened in 1778 on the site of the demolished church of Santa Maria alla Scala. Verdi’s Otello and Puccini’s Madama Butterfly both premiered at the opera house.

storyTitle.en-US: Forty minutes in front of the Last Supper

storyDescription.en-US: Hosts Phil and Laura take apart Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper, painted in the 1490s on the dining-hall wall of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent in an experimental oil-and-tempera technique that began flaking within decades.

locationName.en-US: Last Supper refectory, Santa Maria delle Grazie

storyTitle.en-US: Saffron, a prank and a yellow wedding rice

storyDescription.en-US: Sauced traces risotto alla milanese, Milan’s saffron rice, from saffron fraud in medieval Nuremberg to the story of a glassmaker’s apprentice on the Duomo cathedral’s windows who, legend says, tinted a 1574 wedding risotto yellow as a joke.

storyTitle.en-US: A fashion heir is shot on his office steps

storyDescription.en-US: On 27 March 1995 Maurizio Gucci, former head of the fashion house, was shot dead outside his office on Via Palestro. Rachel Naylor talks to Carmine Gallo, the detective who tied the killing to his ex-wife Patrizia Reggiani and her clairvoyant.

storyTitle.en-US: The Argentine coach who taught Inter to defend

storyDescription.en-US: Football writers Jonathan Wilson and Rob Draper on Helenio Herrera, the Argentine coach whose Inter won the European Cup in 1964 and 1965 with catenaccio, a defence-first system. Inter play at San Siro stadium, which they share with AC Milan.

stories.__iconKey: It Was What It Was : The Football History Podcast

storyTitle.en-US: Sculpted family tombs in the city of the dead

storyDescription.en-US: History Goes Bump, a podcast on haunted history, tours the Cimitero Monumentale, opened in 1866 and filled with sculpted tombs of Milan’s industrial families. Novelist Alessandro Manzoni is buried in its Famedio, a hall of fame by the main gate.

stories.__iconKey: History Goes Bump: Ghost Tours For The Mind

storyTitle.en-US: Art nouveau, Milan style, around Porta Venezia

storyDescription.en-US: Listen To MI, a podcast from Milan’s house museums, looks at Liberty, the Italian art nouveau of about 1900, in the Porta Venezia district. The style’s best-known building there is Giuseppe Sommaruga’s Palazzo Castiglioni on Corso Venezia.

stories.__iconKey: Listen To MI - Milan and its House Museums in a podcast

storyTitle.en-US: An architect’s flats for a couple of collectors

storyDescription.en-US: Architect Piero Portaluppi shaped interwar Milan. This episode visits his buildings that are open to the public, among them the Casa Museo Boschi Di Stefano, a couple’s flat hung floor to ceiling with 20th-century Italian art.

locationName.en-US: Casa Museo Boschi Di Stefano, Via Jan

stories.__iconKey: Listen To MI - Milan and its House Museums in a podcast

storyTitle.en-US: A fake apse less than a metre deep

storyDescription.en-US: Two Renaissance architects in Milan: Filarete, designer of the Ospedale Maggiore hospital, and Donato Bramante. At Santa Maria presso San Satiro church, Bramante painted and modelled a deep choir behind the altar into a wall less than a metre deep.

locationName.en-US: Santa Maria presso San Satiro church

stories.__iconKey: Listen To MI - Milan and its House Museums in a podcast

storyTitle.en-US: A fashion editor invents the concept store

storyDescription.en-US: Carla Sozzani, former fashion magazine editor, tells how she opened 10 Corso Como in 1990, a gallery, bookshop, boutique and café around a courtyard that is often called the first concept store.

stories.__iconKey: Listen To MI - Milan and its House Museums in a podcast

storyTitle.en-US: A poet’s canal and the writers around it

storyDescription.en-US: A literary walk along the Navigli, Milan’s old canals, starting with poet Alda Merini, who lived for decades on the Ripa di Porta Ticinese beside the Naviglio Grande and wrote about the asylum where she spent years.

locationName.en-US: Alda Merini’s home, Naviglio Grande canal

stories.__iconKey: Listen To MI - Milan and its House Museums in a podcast

storyTitle.en-US: Why the furniture world descends on Milan each April

storyDescription.en-US: Editors at the architecture and design magazine Dezeen explain why Milan design week matters: the Salone del Mobile furniture fair at the Fiera Milano grounds in Rho, plus hundreds of satellite shows around the city known as the Fuorisalone.

storyTitle.en-US: A bishop’s fourth-century church, rebuilt in Romanesque brick

storyDescription.en-US: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, founded this basilica in the 380s and lies in its crypt. Smarthistory looks at the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio, whose brick Romanesque church and arcaded forecourt date mostly from the 11th and 12th centuries.

storyTitle.en-US: Leonardo applies for a job and barely mentions painting

storyDescription.en-US: Around 1482 Leonardo da Vinci wrote to Ludovico Sforza, ruler of Milan, offering bridges, cannon and siege engines, with painting near the end. The draft survives in the Codex Atlanticus, kept at the Biblioteca Ambrosiana library.

storyTitle.en-US: A Last Supper painted on a monks’ dining-room wall

storyDescription.en-US: Leonardo painted the Last Supper around 1495–98 in the refectory of the Dominican convent at Santa Maria delle Grazie church. His experimental paint mix began flaking within his lifetime; Smarthistory looks at what survives.

storyTitle.en-US: A dead Christ seen feet-first

storyDescription.en-US: Andrea Mantegna’s Lamentation over the Dead Christ, around 1483, shows the body from the feet in steep foreshortening, mourners squeezed at the edge. It hangs in the Pinacoteca di Brera, the gallery in a former Jesuit college.

storyTitle.en-US: A young Raphael reworks his teacher’s wedding scene

storyDescription.en-US: Raphael was about 21 when he painted the Marriage of the Virgin in 1504 for a church in Città di Castello, reworking a design by his teacher Perugino. It entered the Pinacoteca di Brera art gallery in 1806.

storyTitle.en-US: A duke kneels in armour under a hanging ostrich egg

storyDescription.en-US: Piero della Francesca’s altarpiece shows Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, kneeling in armour before the Virgin, an ostrich egg hanging from the shell-shaped apse. It came from Urbino to the Pinacoteca di Brera gallery in 1811.

storyTitle.en-US: Venetian merchants search Alexandria’s tombs for a saint

storyDescription.en-US: Jacopo Tintoretto painted the Finding of the Body of Saint Mark in the 1560s for a Venetian confraternity, with men pulling corpses from tombs in Alexandria down a deep vaulted hall. It now hangs in Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera gallery.

storyTitle.en-US: Painters in love with speed, machines and the modern city

storyDescription.en-US: Poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti launched Futurism in 1909, and its painters, led by Umberto Boccioni, worked in Milan, celebrating speed, machines and war. The Museo del Novecento, the 20th-century art museum on Piazza del Duomo, holds key works.

locationName.en-US: Museo del Novecento, Piazza del Duomo

storyTitle.en-US: Walking among the spires on the cathedral roof

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves climbs onto the marble roof terraces of the Duomo, Milan’s Gothic cathedral, begun in 1386 and worked on for nearly six centuries, where visitors walk among its forest of spires and statues.

storyTitle.en-US: A marble middle finger faces the stock exchange

storyDescription.en-US: Artist Maurizio Cattelan’s marble hand, L.O.V.E., with every finger cut off but the middle one, has stood since 2010 in Piazza Affari square, facing the 1930s stock exchange. Rick Steves considers who it is meant for.

locationName.en-US: Piazza Affari, outside the stock exchange

storyTitle.en-US: Glass towers and tree-covered flats on old railway land

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves visits Porta Nuova, a business district built on former rail yards in the 2010s, with the spired UniCredit Tower above Piazza Gae Aulenti square and Stefano Boeri’s planted apartment towers, the Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest).

storyTitle.en-US: The city’s uprising against Austria, told in a quiet museum

storyDescription.en-US: The Risorgimento was the 19th-century drive to unify Italy, and Milan’s Five Days revolt against Austrian rule in March 1848 was a turning point. Rick Steves visits the Risorgimento Museum in Palazzo Moriggia, a mansion in Brera.

storyTitle.en-US: Domed concrete igloo homes from the postwar housing crisis

storyDescription.en-US: In 1946 engineer Mario Cavallè built a small estate of domed concrete houses in the Maggiolina neighbourhood as quick postwar housing. The Tim Traveller visits the survivors, on and around Via Lepanto, still lived in today.

storyTitle.en-US: A world’s fair about feeding the planet

storyDescription.en-US: Milan hosted the 2015 World Expo, themed “Feeding the Planet, Energy for Life”, on a new site at Rho on the city’s northwest edge. DW’s lifestyle show Euromaxx tours the national pavilions; the grounds are now the MIND science district.

storyTitle.en-US: Two apartment towers planted with trees

storyDescription.en-US: Architect Stefano Boeri’s Bosco Verticale, two Porta Nuova apartment towers planted with hundreds of trees and finished in 2014. The B1M, a construction channel, asks whether the greenery makes up for the extra concrete and steel needed to carry it.

storyTitle.en-US: Two rival clubs, one ageing stadium

storyDescription.en-US: San Siro, officially the Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, opened in 1926 and is shared by AC Milan and Inter. BBC Sport looks at the clubs’ plans to replace the stadium and what the city stands to lose.

storyTitle.en-US: A duke’s daughter grows up at the Sforza court

storyDescription.en-US: Extra History’s animated series on Caterina Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, starts with her childhood at the ducal court, which lived in the Castello Sforzesco, before marriage took her to Romagna.

storyTitle.en-US: A glass-roofed arcade between cathedral and opera

storyDescription.en-US: Art historian Rocky Ruggiero on the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, the iron-and-glass shopping arcade built from 1865 to 1877 to link the Duomo square with La Scala, named after Italy’s first king.

storyTitle.en-US: A tower shaped like a castle keep rises from bomb damage

storyDescription.en-US: Torre Velasca, the BBPR studio’s 1958 office and apartment tower, its upper floors jutting out like a medieval castle keep, rose on a bomb-damaged site. Architectural Record, the US architecture magazine, tells its postwar story.

storyTitle.en-US: Milan Walking Tour • Duomo and La Scala Secrets with Brera District

storyDescription.en-US: From La Scala opera house to the cobbled lanes and galleries of Brera, the old artists’ quarter, with stories of the people who lived and worked there.

storyTitle.en-US: The Mysteries of Milan: From the Duomo to the Royal Palace

storyDescription.en-US: Legends and odd details around the cathedral square, from the Duomo’s spires to the Royal Palace next door.

storyTitle.en-US: Milan Fashion Tour: A Guide to Quadrilatero della Moda with Context

storyDescription.en-US: A walk through the Quadrilatero della Moda, the block of streets where Milan’s fashion houses keep their flagship shops, and how the city became a fashion capital.

storyTitle.en-US: The Doll

storyDescription.en-US: Prus’s 1890 novel follows Wokulski, a self-made merchant hopelessly in love with an aristocrat. It is Warsaw’s great novel, and it’s long. A plaque on Krakowskie Przedmieście, the royal road, marks the house where readers placed his shop.

storyTitle.en-US: Obsessive Genius: The Inner World of Marie Curie

storyDescription.en-US: A short, clear life of the physicist Marie Curie, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. She was born Maria Skłodowska in 1867 in a house on Freta Street in the New Town, now a small museum, and studied in secret classes under Russian rule.

storyTitle.en-US: In My Father’s Court

storyDescription.en-US: Nobel novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer remembers his boyhood at No. 10 Krochmalna Street, where his rabbi father settled the neighbours’ quarrels. The poor Jewish street of thieves, tailors and widows was destroyed in the war. The street name survives.

storyTitle.en-US: The King of Children: The Life and Death of Janusz Korczak

storyDescription.en-US: Janusz Korczak was a doctor and children’s author who ran a Jewish orphanage. In 1942 he refused rescue and went with his 200 children to the deportation trains. His orphanage on Jaktorowska Street still stands, and is still a children’s home.

storyTitle.en-US: The Zookeeper’s Wife

storyDescription.en-US: Antonina Żabińska and her husband Jan, director of Warsaw Zoo, hid about 300 Jews in empty cages and their own house during the German occupation. Their villa inside the zoo in Praga, across the Vistula river, is open to visitors.

storyTitle.en-US: The Pianist

storyDescription.en-US: Pianist Władysław Szpilman’s plain account of surviving the ghetto, then hiding alone in the ruined city, helped at the end by a German officer. Published in 1946, it was reissued only in 1998. A piece of the ghetto wall survives on Sienna Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Shielding the Flame

storyDescription.en-US: Journalist Hanna Krall interviews Marek Edelman, the last surviving commander of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, who became a heart surgeon. He talks flatly, with no heroics. The fighters’ last bunker at Miła 18 is now a grassy mound with a stone.

storyTitle.en-US: Rising ’44: The Battle for Warsaw

storyDescription.en-US: British historian Norman Davies on the Warsaw Uprising, the Home Army’s 63-day revolt against German occupation in 1944, while the Soviets waited across the river. It’s long and openly partisan. The Warsaw Rising Museum fills an old tram power station.

storyTitle.en-US: A Memoir of the Warsaw Uprising

storyDescription.en-US: Poet Miron Białoszewski’s record of the Uprising from the cellars, where civilians queued for water and moved from ruin to ruin. No battles, just daily life under bombs. The Old Town around its market square was flattened that summer and rebuilt by 1953.

storyTitle.en-US: Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe 1944–1956

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Anne Applebaum on how Soviet-backed communists took over Poland, Hungary and East Germany after the war. Warsaw’s Constitution Square, built around 1952 with giant stone workers on its facades, is that era set in stone.

storyTitle.en-US: A Minor Apocalypse

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist Tadeusz Konwicki’s dark comedy: a writer is asked to burn himself alive outside the Communist Party’s offices and spends a day wandering Warsaw’s shortages and queues. It ends at the Palace of Culture and Science, Stalin’s 1955 gift to the city.

storyTitle.en-US: Who Will Write Our History

storyDescription.en-US: Documentary with re-enactments about historian Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret group, which buried an archive of ghetto life in milk cans. Two of its three caches were dug up after the war. Parts are on show at the Jewish Historical Institute.

storyTitle.en-US: The Zookeeper’s Wife

storyDescription.en-US: Jessica Chastain plays Antonina Żabińska, who with her husband Jan sheltered Jews in Warsaw Zoo during the occupation. Shot in Prague, not Warsaw. The real zoo is in Praga, the district on the Vistula’s east bank, and the Żabińskis’ villa is open.

storyTitle.en-US: The Pianist

storyDescription.en-US: Roman Polański’s film of Władysław Szpilman’s memoir, with Adrien Brody as the pianist. In 1942 his family was sent from the Umschlagplatz, the ghetto’s railway loading yard, to Treblinka. A white marble memorial stands there on Stawki Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Warsaw Uprising

storyDescription.en-US: Real colour and black-and-white footage shot by Home Army cameramen in 1944, edited into a story of two young reporters, with voices added by lip-readers. Made by Jan Komasa with the Warsaw Rising Museum, which shows the original reels.

storyTitle.en-US: Kanał

storyDescription.en-US: Andrzej Wajda’s film about a Home Army company escaping through the sewers (kanały) as the 1944 Uprising collapses. Bleak and short. On Dworkowa Street a memorial marks the manhole where Germans shot more than 100 insurgents as they climbed out.

storyTitle.en-US: The Cruise

storyDescription.en-US: Marek Piwowski’s cult comedy, originally Rejs. Stowaways on a Vistula pleasure boat elect a committee and hold absurd meetings, a sly picture of communist life. Mostly amateur actors. Poles quote it constantly. The boat sails from Warsaw’s riverbank.

storyTitle.en-US: 4 Alternative Street

storyDescription.en-US: Stanisław Bareja’s TV satire, originally Alternatywy 4: a petty building caretaker bullies the tenants of a new tower block. Censors held it back until 1986. It was shot in the big concrete estates of Ursynów, in south Warsaw. Nine episodes.

storyTitle.en-US: Leave No Traces

storyDescription.en-US: In 1983 militia officers beat student Grzegorz Przemyk to death in a police station on Jezuicka Street, in the Old Town. The state then spent years covering it up. This film follows the friend who saw it. Long, at nearly three hours.

locationName.en-US: Jezuicka Street police station, Old Town

storyTitle.en-US: Dekalog

storyDescription.en-US: Krzysztof Kieślowski’s ten one-hour films, each loosely on one of the Ten Commandments, about people in a single grey 1980s housing estate. Shot on the Stawki estate on the edge of Muranów, built over the ruins of the ghetto.

storyTitle.en-US: A Film Unfinished

storyDescription.en-US: Israeli director Yael Hersonski examines ‘Das Ghetto’, unfinished Nazi propaganda film shot in the Warsaw ghetto in 1942, setting staged scenes against survivors’ accounts. On Chłodna Street, light poles mark the footbridge joining the ghetto’s two parts.

storyTitle.en-US: Popiełuszko: Freedom Is Within Us

storyDescription.en-US: Biopic of Jerzy Popiełuszko, the priest whose ‘Masses for the Homeland’ drew thousands of Solidarity supporters until secret police officers murdered him in 1984. He is buried at St Stanisław Kostka Church in Żoliborz, where he served.

storyTitle.en-US: Saviour Square

storyDescription.en-US: A young family loses its savings when the developer of its new flat goes bust, and moves in with a domineering mother-in-law. Bleak and hard-going. Fiction, named for the round square of arcaded 1950s blocks around the Church of the Holiest Saviour.

storyTitle.en-US: Stones for the Rampart

storyDescription.en-US: Drawn from Aleksander Kamiński’s 1943 book about real scouts in the Home Army underground. Its climax is Operation Arsenal, the March 1943 raid by the Arsenal on Długa Street that freed Jan Bytnar from a Gestapo truck. He died of his torture days later.

storyTitle.en-US: Polonaise in A-flat major, Op. 53 “Heroic”

storyDescription.en-US: Chopin grew up in Warsaw and left at 20, never to return. His heart did: his sister smuggled it home, and it rests in a pillar of Holy Cross Church. This stirring polonaise, a Polish court dance, became a wartime emblem of national pride.

storyTitle.en-US: Halka: Mazur

storyDescription.en-US: Halka, by composer Stanisław Moniuszko, is the founding Polish national opera: a highland girl seduced and abandoned by a nobleman. Its full version premiered in Warsaw’s Grand Theatre in 1858; his statue stands outside. The mazur is a quick Polish dance.

storyTitle.en-US: Ta ostatnia niedziela

storyDescription.en-US: “This Last Sunday,” Jerzy Petersburski’s tango of a final farewell, was a 1935 hit for Warsaw crooner Mieczysław Fogg. Petersburski led a band at the Adria, the interwar city’s smartest dance hall; Fogg later sang for fighters in the 1944 uprising.

storyTitle.en-US: Kattorna

storyDescription.en-US: Pianist Krzysztof Komeda, who scored Roman Polanski’s early films, recorded his album Astigmatic at the National Philharmonic hall in December 1965. Often called the high point of Polish jazz, it opens with this theme from a Danish film.

storyTitle.en-US: Sen o Warszawie

storyDescription.en-US: “A Dream of Warsaw”: singer Czesław Niemen’s soaring song of longing to return to the city. Fans of Legia, Warsaw’s main football club, adopted it as their anthem and sing it en masse at the club’s stadium on Łazienkowska street.

storyTitle.en-US: Warszawa

storyDescription.en-US: In 1976 David Bowie’s train stopped at Warszawa Gdańska station and he walked the grey streets nearby, buying records of Polish folk music. The wordless chant he sang with Brian Eno on the album Low borrows from one of those folk songs.

storyTitle.en-US: Mniej niż zero

storyDescription.en-US: “Less Than Zero” made Warsaw band Lady Pank, led by guitarist Jan Borysewicz, stars under martial law. It topped the weekly chart of Polish Radio Three, the station that gave a generation its rock, broadcast from this building on Myśliwiecka street.

locationName.en-US: Polish Radio Three building, Myśliwiecka street

storyTitle.en-US: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23 (The Pianist)

storyDescription.en-US: Pianist Janusz Olejniczak played the Chopin heard in Roman Polanski’s The Pianist. Władysław Szpilman, a Jewish pianist who escaped the Warsaw Ghetto, survived hiding in a ruined house at Niepodległości avenue 223, where a German officer found him.

storyTitle.en-US: Ukryty w mieście krzyk

storyDescription.en-US: “A Cry Hidden in the City,” from rapper Pezet and producer Noon’s album Muzyka klasyczna, is a moody night drive through Warsaw. Pezet came up in Ursynów, the vast 1970s concrete housing district on the southern edge of the city that bred its rap scene.

storyTitle.en-US: Godzina W

storyDescription.en-US: “W-Hour” was 5 pm on 1 August 1944, when the Home Army began the Warsaw Uprising, a 63-day revolt against German occupation. Rock band Lao Che made a whole album about it, launched at the Warsaw Rising Museum, which hosts their anniversary concerts.

storyTitle.en-US: Następna stacja

storyDescription.en-US: “Next Station,” from Warsaw rapper Taco Hemingway’s EP Umowa o dzieło, borrows the metro announcer’s phrase for a ride across a city of hustle and fatigue. Świętokrzyska is the downtown station where the two Warsaw metro lines meet.

storyTitle.en-US: Patointeligencja

storyDescription.en-US: The title is slang for “pathological intelligentsia”: Mata, a 19-year-old pupil at the elite Stefan Batory High School, rapped about rich Warsaw teenagers’ drugs and boredom. The song set off a national row and topped the Polish charts.

locationName.en-US: Stefan Batory High School, Myśliwiecka street

storyTitle.en-US: Szampan

storyDescription.en-US: “Champagne,” a breezy hit by Warsaw-born singer Sanah (Zuzanna Grabowska), a classically trained violinist. On 22 September 2023 she became the first Polish woman to sell out the National Stadium, the bowl-shaped arena on the Vistula’s east bank.

storyTitle.en-US: Rebuilding the Old Town from 18th-century paintings

storyDescription.en-US: German forces levelled Warsaw’s Old Town after the 1944 Uprising. 99% Invisible, Roman Mars’s design show, tells how it was rebuilt from the 1940s using 18th-century views of the city by the painter Bernardo Bellotto, known as Canaletto.

storyTitle.en-US: A girl from Freta Street becomes the first woman to win a Nobel

storyDescription.en-US: Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 on Freta Street in the New Town, studied at Warsaw’s illegal ‘Flying University’ and left for Paris, where she discovered polonium and radium. Her birthplace is now a small museum to her life.

storyTitle.en-US: A city besieged for three weeks in September 1939

storyDescription.en-US: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook on the German siege of Warsaw in 1939, when shelling and bombing set the Royal Castle on Castle Square ablaze, and the city’s surrender on 28 September after nearly three weeks of resistance.

storyTitle.en-US: Sixty-three days of fighting for a city the Red Army watched

storyDescription.en-US: On 1 August 1944 the Home Army, Poland’s underground resistance, rose against the German occupiers and held out for 63 days while Soviet forces halted across the Vistula. The Warsaw Rising Museum, in an old tram power station in Wola, tells the story.

storyTitle.en-US: Civilians killed street by street in the Uprising’s first week

storyDescription.en-US: In early August 1944, days into the Warsaw Uprising, German and collaborating units shot tens of thousands of civilians in the western district of Wola. History Hit’s Warfare show covers the massacre; a memorial now stands on Leszno Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Moscow signs up its satellites in a Warsaw palace

storyDescription.en-US: On 14 May 1955 the Soviet Union and seven Eastern Bloc states signed a military alliance in Warsaw, a reply to West Germany joining NATO. The BBC’s Witness History hears the story; the treaty was signed in what is now the Presidential Palace.

storyTitle.en-US: Warsaw’s turning points, with a historian of its ruin

storyDescription.en-US: Travel journalist Paul Bloomfield talks to historian Alexandra Richie, author of a history of the 1944 Uprising, on the turning points of Warsaw’s past. The Barbican, a 16th-century gate tower rebuilt after 1945, guards the Old Town’s north side.

storyTitle.en-US: A republic that elected its kings

storyDescription.en-US: Melvyn Bragg and guests on the union of Poland and Lithuania, formalised in 1569, whose nobles elected their kings. One of them, Jan III Sobieski, victor over the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683, built Wilanów Palace as his summer residence.

storyTitle.en-US: The Rolling Stones play behind the Iron Curtain

storyDescription.en-US: Culture.pl’s podcast on the Rolling Stones’ April 1967 concert in Warsaw, one of the first by a Western rock band in the Soviet bloc. Fans without tickets clashed with police outside the Congress Hall, the venue inside Stalin’s Palace of Culture.

locationName.en-US: Congress Hall, Palace of Culture and Science

storyTitle.en-US: Smuggling children out of the ghetto

storyDescription.en-US: Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker, used her pass into the Warsaw ghetto to smuggle out Jewish children for Żegota, the underground aid council, and buried their names in jars. A stretch of the ghetto wall survives in a courtyard off Sienna Street.

stories.__iconKey: Witness History: World War Two history

storyTitle.en-US: A ghetto fighter who led survivors out through the sewers

storyDescription.en-US: Simha ‘Kazik’ Rotem, who guided fighters out through the sewers as the Germans crushed the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, tells his story. The mound at Miła 18 marks the bunker where the uprising’s commander, Mordechai Anielewicz, died.

stories.__iconKey: Witness History: World War Two history

storyTitle.en-US: Students against the censors, March 1968

storyDescription.en-US: After the authorities banned a staging of Adam Mickiewicz’s play ‘Forefathers’ Eve’, University of Warsaw students rallied for free speech in March 1968 and were beaten by police. Their protests began at the university’s gate on Krakowskie Przedmieście.

storyTitle.en-US: The plane crash that killed a president

storyDescription.en-US: In April 2010 a plane carrying President Lech Kaczyński and 95 others crashed near Smolensk in Russia, on the way to a Katyn massacre commemoration. Radosław Sikorski, then foreign minister, recalls the day. A memorial stands on Piłsudski Square.

storyTitle.en-US: Teenage scouts in the 1944 Uprising

storyDescription.en-US: A former scout recalls the Warsaw Uprising of 1944, the Home Army’s revolt against German occupation, in which boys and girls ran messages, mail and ammunition. The Little Insurgent statue on Podwale Street honours the child fighters.

stories.__iconKey: Witness History: World War Two history

storyTitle.en-US: A city that put its own centre back together

storyDescription.en-US: American travel writer Rick Steves on how Warsaw, about 85 per cent destroyed by 1945, rebuilt itself. Castle Square, with King Sigismund III’s column and the reconstructed Royal Castle, is where the rebuilt Old Town begins.

storyTitle.en-US: Monuments to the fighters of 1944

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves looks at how Warsaw remembers its dead and rebuilt its streets. The Warsaw Uprising Monument on Krasiński Square, unveiled in 1989, shows insurgents climbing down into the sewers they used to move between districts.

storyTitle.en-US: Chopin, and the national spirit

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves on two Polish passions, vodka and the composer Fryderyk Chopin, who grew up in Warsaw and left for Paris in 1830. The Chopin Museum in the Ostrogski Palace holds his last piano and manuscripts.

storyTitle.en-US: Daffodils for the ghetto fighters, eighty years on

storyDescription.en-US: In April 1943 Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto, the walled district where the Nazis confined the city’s Jews, rose against deportation to Treblinka. BBC News reports on the 2023 commemoration at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes in Muranów.

storyTitle.en-US: The tower Stalin gave Warsaw

storyDescription.en-US: Megaprojects, an engineering history channel, on the Palace of Culture and Science, Stalin’s ‘gift’ built by Soviet workers in 1952–55. At 237 metres with its spire it was long Poland’s tallest building, and many Varsovians still resent it.

storyTitle.en-US: Old shop signs saved from the scrapheap

storyDescription.en-US: TVP World, Poland’s English-language public broadcaster, talks to David Hill, co-founder of the Neon Muzeum, which rescues cold-war neon signs from Warsaw’s shops and cafés. It fills a former factory hall in the Soho Factory complex in Praga.

storyTitle.en-US: The last king’s bathhouse palace

storyDescription.en-US: TVP World’s ‘Pulse of Culture’ tours Royal Łazienki, the park of Poland’s last king, Stanisław August Poniatowski. Łazienki means ‘baths’: its Palace on the Isle began as a bathhouse that he turned into a summer palace in the 1780s.

locationName.en-US: Palace on the Isle, Łazienki Park

storyTitle.en-US: Socialist realism on Constitution Square

storyDescription.en-US: Radosław Gajda explains MDM, the Marszałkowska Residential District built in 1950–52 in socialist realism, the Soviet-imposed official style. Its showpiece, Constitution Square, has arcades, giant lamp standards and reliefs of model workers.

storyTitle.en-US: The 1920 battle Poles call a miracle

storyDescription.en-US: The History Guy, an American history channel, on the Battle of Warsaw in August 1920, when Polish forces stopped the Red Army near the capital: the ‘Miracle on the Vistula’. Józef Piłsudski, Poland’s head of state, then lived in Belweder Palace.

stories.__iconKey: The History Guy: History Deserves to Be Remembered

storyTitle.en-US: A café where Warsaw’s poets held court

storyDescription.en-US: POLIN, the museum of Polish Jewish history, visits the site of Mała Ziemiańska, the interwar café on Mazowiecka Street where poets such as Julian Tuwim and Antoni Słonimski held court. It was destroyed in 1944.

locationName.en-US: Site of Mała Ziemiańska café, Mazowiecka Street

storyTitle.en-US: The ghetto, told by the museum that will house its story

storyDescription.en-US: The Warsaw Ghetto Museum’s account of the ghetto, sealed in November 1940, where some 400,000 Jews were confined. The museum is moving into the Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital on Sienna Street, one of the few ghetto buildings left.

locationName.en-US: Warsaw Ghetto Museum, former Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital

storyTitle.en-US: A Miracle from the Rubble: Warsaw Old Town Walking Tour

storyDescription.en-US: A history of the Old Town’s destruction in 1944 and its rebuilding, past the reconstructed royal castle, the Jesuit church and cathedral, the main market square and the city’s brick defensive gate, ending at a lookout over the Vistula river.

storyTitle.en-US: Krakowskie Przedmieście: The fascinating story of the street

storyDescription.en-US: A history of the city’s grandest street, starting at the main entrance of the royal castle and heading south past the statue of the national poet and the old palace that now houses the university, along the old road to Kraków.

storyTitle.en-US: Warsaw at War: 1939-1945

storyDescription.en-US: A Second World War history of Warsaw from the German invasion of 1939 to the city’s destruction in 1945, passing the musical benches that play the composer Chopin’s works.

storyTitle.en-US: Łazienki Park: Legacy of the Last King

storyDescription.en-US: A walk through the royal bathhouse park laid out by Poland’s last king, Stanisław August Poniatowski, taking in the story of the warrior king who beat the Ottomans at Vienna, and the monument to the composer Chopin.

storyTitle.en-US: Wilanów Palace: Legacy of King Jan III Sobieski

storyDescription.en-US: A royal history tour of the baroque summer palace built by King Jan III Sobieski, who broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, telling the story of his 1683 victory at the palace on the city’s southern edge.

storyTitle.en-US: From Stalin to Skyscrapers: A Walk Around Warsaw’s Palace of Culture

storyDescription.en-US: An architecture and politics walk around the Soviet-built tower Stalin gave the city in 1955, crossing the vast parade ground at its foot and ending among the glass office towers that have grown up around it since communism fell.

storyTitle.en-US: Surprised by Joy

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist C. S. Lewis on his early life, starting in a big, book-crammed house in East Belfast where he and his brother invented imaginary worlds. C. S. Lewis Square, a plaza nearby, has bronze figures from the Narnia books.

locationName.en-US: C. S. Lewis Square, East Belfast

storyTitle.en-US: Thomas Andrews: Shipbuilder

storyDescription.en-US: A short life of Thomas Andrews, the Harland & Wolff designer who went down with the Titanic in 1912, written by novelist Shan Bullock that same year. Andrews worked in the shipyard’s drawing offices. The building is now a hotel.

storyTitle.en-US: These Days

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist Lucy Caldwell follows two sisters through the German air raids of spring 1941, the Belfast Blitz. Around 900 people died in one April night, many in the packed streets of North Belfast around York Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Immortal: The Approved Biography of George Best

storyDescription.en-US: Sportswriter Duncan Hamilton on footballer George Best, who left the Cregagh housing estate at 15 for Manchester United and became football’s first pop-star celebrity. Drink ended his career early. The city airport now carries his name.

storyTitle.en-US: The Lonely Passion of Judith Hearne

storyDescription.en-US: Brian Moore’s first novel: a lonely, devout piano teacher in a shabby boarding house in the streets near Queen’s University, where respectability was everything. Moore left Belfast and never moved back. A fiction pick; the city is its subject.

storyTitle.en-US: The Star Factory

storyDescription.en-US: Poet Ciaran Carson’s memoir of growing up Irish-speaking off the Falls Road in the 1950s. It wanders from street names to old factories and his postman father’s stories. The title comes from a shirt factory near the family home on Raglan Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Milkman

storyDescription.en-US: Anna Burns’s Booker winner: a teenager stalked by a paramilitary in the 1970s, during the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s future. Nothing is named, but it draws on Ardoyne, the north Belfast district where Burns grew up.

storyTitle.en-US: Say Nothing

storyDescription.en-US: Journalist Patrick Radden Keefe on Jean McConville, a widowed mother of ten taken from her flat by the IRA in 1972 and killed. Her body was found in 2003. Divis Tower is the last surviving block of the Divis Flats estate where she lived.

storyTitle.en-US: Northern Protestants: An Unsettled People

storyDescription.en-US: Journalist Susan McKay, herself from a Protestant family, interviews unionists and loyalists about faith, fear and belonging. It is the counterweight to books about the republican side. The Shankill Road is the heart of loyalist West Belfast.

storyTitle.en-US: Eureka Street

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist Robert McLiam Wilson’s comedy about two friends, one Catholic and one Protestant, in Belfast around the 1994 ceasefires. It is funny until a bomb goes off a few streets from City Hall, the domed civic building at the centre.

storyTitle.en-US: Odd Man Out

storyDescription.en-US: Director Carol Reed’s film about a wounded gunman (James Mason) hunted through the city on his last night. Partly shot in Belfast. Its pub scenes copy the Crown Liquor Saloon, the Victorian gin palace on Great Victoria Street, still pouring today.

locationName.en-US: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street

storyTitle.en-US: Belfast

storyDescription.en-US: Actor-director Kenneth Branagh’s account of his own childhood in 1969, when riots broke out and his family weighed leaving. Shot in black and white. Branagh grew up on Mountcollyer Street in north Belfast; the family left for England when he was nine.

Director Yann Demange’s thriller about a young British soldier stranded in West Belfast after a riot in 1971, early in the Troubles. Fiction, filmed in England. The peace wall on Cupar Way still separates the Catholic Falls from the Protestant Shankill.

storyTitle.en-US: Good Vibrations

storyDescription.en-US: Comedy-drama about Terri Hooley, who opened a record shop and label in the 1970s and put out the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks”. Punk crossed sectarian lines. The Harp Bar on Hill Street, now in the Cathedral Quarter nightlife area, was the scene’s home.

creatorName.en-US: Lisa Barros D’Sa and Glenn Leyburn

storyTitle.en-US: Hunger

storyDescription.en-US: Artist Steve McQueen’s first feature, about IRA prisoner Bobby Sands, who starved himself to death in the Maze prison in 1981 aged 27. Hard to watch, with long silent stretches. His mural is on the side of the Sinn Féin office on the Falls Road.

storyTitle.en-US: The Fall

storyDescription.en-US: BBC crime series with Gillian Anderson as a London detective hunting a serial killer (Jamie Dornan) who poses as a family man. A rare Belfast story not about the Troubles. Much of it plays out in the well-off south of the city around Malone Road.

storyTitle.en-US: Kneecap

storyDescription.en-US: Writer-director Rich Peppiatt’s loosely true comedy about Kneecap, a West Belfast hip-hop trio who rap in Irish and play themselves. Crude and political. The Cultúrlann, an Irish-language arts centre on the Falls Road, is a hub of the revival they rap for.

locationName.en-US: Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich, Falls Road

storyTitle.en-US: Titanic Town

storyDescription.en-US: Julie Walters plays a mother in 1972 Andersonstown, a Catholic estate in west Belfast, who starts a peace campaign and ends up despised by the IRA and the British Army alike. From Mary Costello’s novel based on her own mother. Funny as often as grim.

storyTitle.en-US: Framing John DeLorean

storyDescription.en-US: Documentary with dramatised scenes, Alec Baldwin as carmaker John DeLorean, whose gull-winged DMC-12 was built with British government money at a factory in Dunmurry on Belfast’s edge. It closed in 1982, the year of his arrest on drug charges.

creatorName.en-US: Don Argott and Sheena M. Joyce

storyTitle.en-US: George Best: All by Himself

storyDescription.en-US: Daniel Gordon’s documentary on footballer George Best, from the Cregagh estate in east Belfast to Manchester United stardom and a long fall into alcoholism. He won 37 caps for Northern Ireland, whose home ground is Windsor Park stadium.

storyTitle.en-US: My Lagan Love

storyDescription.en-US: Belfast poet Joseph Campbell wrote the words and Belfast-born composer Herbert Hughes published the air in 1904, a lament for a girl by the River Lagan. Kate Bush recorded it in 1989; the river meets the city at Lagan Weir.

storyTitle.en-US: Softly, Softly

storyDescription.en-US: Ruby Murray, raised off the Donegall Road in south Belfast, took this ballad to No. 1 in Britain in 1955 and once had five singles in the Top 20 in the same week. Belfast unveiled a blue plaque to her in 2019.

storyTitle.en-US: Gloria

storyDescription.en-US: Them, the band fronted by a teenage Van Morrison, built this three-chord stomp in their residency at the Maritime Hotel’s R&B club. Countless garage bands copied it; the old seamen’s hotel on College Square North is long gone.

storyTitle.en-US: Cyprus Avenue

storyDescription.en-US: Van Morrison, born a mile away on Hyndford Street, turned this leafy, well-off east Belfast avenue into the centrepiece of his 1968 album Astral Weeks. In 2015 he played a 70th-birthday concert on the street itself.

storyTitle.en-US: Belfast Boy

storyDescription.en-US: English singer Don Fardon’s tribute to footballer George Best, the Manchester United winger who grew up on the Cregagh council estate in east Belfast. Best’s boyhood home on Burren Way is still visited by fans.

storyTitle.en-US: Stairway to Heaven

storyDescription.en-US: Led Zeppelin, the London rock band, played this song live for the first time at the Ulster Hall on 5 March 1971, months before it came out on record. The Victorian concert hall on Bedford Street still hosts gigs.

storyTitle.en-US: Big Time

storyDescription.en-US: Belfast punks Rudi made this the first single on Good Vibrations, the label run by record-shop owner Terri Hooley from Great Victoria Street. His shop gave young fans a scene across the sectarian divide during the Troubles.

locationName.en-US: Good Vibrations record shop, Great Victoria Street

storyTitle.en-US: Alternative Ulster

storyDescription.en-US: Stiff Little Fingers, from Belfast, shouted about life under the Troubles, the decades of conflict over Northern Ireland’s future, with soldiers on every corner. Punks crowded the Harp Bar on Hill Street to hear bands like them.

storyTitle.en-US: Annie’s Song

storyDescription.en-US: Flautist James Galway, who grew up in working-class north Belfast and learned in local flute bands, took this instrumental of John Denver’s love song to No. 3 in Britain. The pin is the York Road, spine of his old district.

storyTitle.en-US: I’ll Tell Me Ma

storyDescription.en-US: A children’s skipping song whose chorus crowns “the belle of Belfast city”; Van Morrison recorded it with Irish folk group the Chieftains on Irish Heartbeat. Belfast City Hall, the domed civic heart of the city, stands for her.

storyTitle.en-US: Glue

storyDescription.en-US: Belfast DJ duo Bicep wrote this wistful track out of nostalgia for 1990s rave. Shine, the long-running club night at Queen’s University Students’ Union, anchored the Belfast dance scene they grew up in.

storyTitle.en-US: C.E.A.R.T.A.

storyDescription.en-US: The title means “rights.” West Belfast rap trio Kneecap rhyme in Irish and English about a member refusing to speak English to police. Their Irish-language scene centres on Cultúrlann, an arts centre on the Falls Road.

locationName.en-US: Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich, Falls Road

storyTitle.en-US: One of the old town’s first streets, end to end

storyDescription.en-US: The Historical Belfast podcast explores North Street, one of the old town’s original thoroughfares, running from the city centre past the Cathedral Quarter, the arts and nightlife district around St Anne’s Cathedral.

storyTitle.en-US: A German-born linen baron is hounded out of the city he served

storyDescription.en-US: Sir Otto Jaffe, a German-Jewish linen merchant, was twice Lord Mayor of Belfast and built its synagogue, yet anti-German feeling in the First World War drove him out. His family’s memorial fountain now stands in Victoria Square.

stories.__iconKey: Best Of Belfast: Northern Ireland's #1 Interview Podcast

storyTitle.en-US: The biggest ship in the world takes shape on the Lagan

storyDescription.en-US: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin their series on the Titanic, built from 1909 to 1911 at Harland & Wolff shipyard. Its slipway on Queen’s Island now lies beside the Titanic Belfast museum.

storyTitle.en-US: Unionist leaders gather at a mansion to defy Home Rule

storyDescription.en-US: Craigavon House in east Belfast, home of unionist leader James Craig, was where Edward Carson rallied crowds against Irish Home Rule in 1911 and where loyalist volunteers drilled. Carol Walker of the Somme Association tells its story.

storyTitle.en-US: A Catholic family is murdered in their home in 1922

storyDescription.en-US: In March 1922, amid the violence that followed Ireland’s partition, gunmen broke into publican Owen McMahon’s house on Kinnaird Terrace off the Antrim Road and killed six men. Historian Edward Burke examines who was behind it.

storyTitle.en-US: Victorian Belfast laid out for the dead, divided underground

storyDescription.en-US: Tom Hartley, a former Lord Mayor and author of a history of Belfast City Cemetery on the Falls Road, walks its graves of linen barons, shipbuilders and the poor, and the sunken wall said to separate Catholic and Protestant plots.

storyTitle.en-US: German bombers find a city with almost no shelters

storyDescription.en-US: German raids in April and May 1941 killed about 1,000 people in Belfast; the Easter Tuesday raid alone was the deadliest night outside London. Historian Dan Snow covers the attacks, which hit north Belfast’s terraces and mills around York Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Walls built as a stopgap in 1969 are still standing

storyDescription.en-US: Belfast’s “peace lines” are barriers between Catholic and Protestant streets, first put up after rioting burned Bombay Street in 1969. Roman Mars’s design show 99% Invisible asks why there are more of them now than in 1998.

storyTitle.en-US: Twenty IRA bombs go off in an afternoon

storyDescription.en-US: On 21 July 1972, during the Troubles (the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s status), the IRA set off about 20 bombs across Belfast in 75 minutes, killing nine. The Belfast Telegraph’s podcast revisits the day and the Oxford Street bus station blast.

storyTitle.en-US: A record-shop owner gives Belfast punk somewhere to go

storyDescription.en-US: Terri Hooley opened the Good Vibrations record shop and label in 1976 and released the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks.” Music writer Stuart Bailie talks about Hooley’s life, and the punk scene that crossed sectarian lines at the height of the Troubles.

locationName.en-US: Good Vibrations record shop, Great Victoria Street

storyTitle.en-US: A gunman attacks mourners at an IRA funeral

storyDescription.en-US: In March 1988, loyalist Michael Stone threw grenades and fired into the crowd at the funeral of three IRA members in Milltown Cemetery on the Falls Road, killing three. BBC Witness History hears from people who were there.

storyTitle.en-US: A Nobel poet’s Belfast years at Queen’s

storyDescription.en-US: Comedian Frank Skinner reads and talks through poems by Seamus Heaney, who studied English at Queen’s University Belfast in the 1950s, taught there and joined the Belfast Group of writers before moving south in 1972.

storyTitle.en-US: Women talk their way into the peace negotiations

storyDescription.en-US: Academic Monica McWilliams co-founded the Northern Ireland Women’s Coalition in 1996, won seats at the peace talks and helped write the 1998 agreement. She went on to sit in the Assembly at Parliament Buildings on the Stormont estate.

storyTitle.en-US: A deal is struck on Good Friday 1998

storyDescription.en-US: After all-night talks at Castle Buildings on the Stormont estate, most of Northern Ireland’s parties and the British and Irish governments approved the Good Friday Agreement on 10 April 1998, the deal that largely ended the Troubles.

storyTitle.en-US: The man at the door of Europe’s most-bombed hotel

storyDescription.en-US: Martin Mulholland, longtime head concierge of the Europa Hotel on Great Victoria Street, talks about decades at a hotel bombed some 30 times in the Troubles, where journalists, presidents and celebrities have stayed.

stories.__iconKey: Best Of Belfast: Northern Ireland's #1 Interview Podcast

storyTitle.en-US: Belfast radicals start a republican movement

storyDescription.en-US: Melvyn Bragg’s In Our Time on the 1798 rising led by the United Irishmen, a society founded by Belfast Presbyterian radicals in 1791. Henry Joy McCracken, hanged in the city that July, is remembered in Clifton Street Cemetery.

storyTitle.en-US: Cups of Armada gold come ashore in a museum

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Suzannah Lipscomb and Michael B. Barry on the Spanish Armada ships wrecked on Ireland’s coast in 1588. Gold and jewels raised from one of them, the Girona, lost off the Antrim coast, are shown at the Ulster Museum.

storyTitle.en-US: A city library older than the city hall

storyDescription.en-US: Julie Andrews, director of the Linen Hall Library, talks about Belfast’s oldest cultural institution, founded in 1788 and now in a Victorian linen warehouse facing City Hall. Its first librarian was United Irishman Thomas Russell.

locationName.en-US: Linen Hall Library, Donegall Square North

storyTitle.en-US: An orphan from Belfast becomes a society painter

storyDescription.en-US: Painter Sir John Lavery, born in Belfast in 1856 and orphaned young, became a leading portraitist of his day, painting Churchill and Michael Collins. He was baptised in St Patrick’s Church on Donegall Street, which holds a triptych he gave it.

stories.__iconKey: Best Of Belfast: Northern Ireland's #1 Interview Podcast

storyTitle.en-US: Shipyard workers win a cup in Vienna

storyDescription.en-US: Just before the First World War, a Glentoran FC side of industrial workers from Ballymacarrett, the terraced district by the shipyards, travelled to Vienna and won its cup. Sam Robinson tells the story. Glentoran still plays at The Oval stadium.

storyTitle.en-US: A heart doctor puts a defibrillator in an ambulance

storyDescription.en-US: In 1966 cardiologist Frank Pantridge of Belfast’s Royal Victoria Hospital launched the world’s first mobile coronary care unit, an ambulance carrying a portable defibrillator run off car batteries. BBC Witness History tells how it started.

storyTitle.en-US: Van Morrison’s east Belfast, street by street

storyDescription.en-US: In the opening segment of Rick Steves’ radio show, a Belfast guide points out the places that shaped singer Van Morrison, born in 1945 at 125 Hyndford Street in east Belfast, and the streets and parks he named in his songs.

storyTitle.en-US: A Belfast boy grows up to define absolute zero

storyDescription.en-US: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, was born on College Square East in 1824 and went on to set the absolute temperature scale and help lay the first working transatlantic telegraph cable. A plaque marks the house; his statue stands in Botanic Gardens.

locationName.en-US: Lord Kelvin’s birthplace, College Square East

stories.__channel: Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution
stories.__iconKey: Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution

storyTitle.en-US: The firm behind the shipyard’s drawing offices

storyDescription.en-US: A history of Harland & Wolff, founded in 1861 by Edward Harland and Gustav Wolff and once the world’s largest shipyard. Titanic was designed in its headquarters drawing offices, now the Titanic Hotel.

storyTitle.en-US: A boss rigger remembers forty years at Harland & Wolff

storyDescription.en-US: George McAllister, a rigger at Harland & Wolff from 1948 to 1992, recalls shipyard work in its later decades, the era when the yard put up Samson and Goliath, the yellow gantry cranes that still dominate the Belfast skyline.

storyTitle.en-US: A black cab ride past the Falls Road murals

storyDescription.en-US: Travel writer Rick Steves rides a black taxi up the Falls Road, the main street of Catholic, nationalist west Belfast, past political murals and memorials to the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s status.

storyTitle.en-US: Orange sashes and bowler hats on parade

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves watches an Orange Order parade, the Protestant fraternity’s marches with bands and banners that peak on the Twelfth of July, marking William of Orange’s 1690 victory. Belfast’s main parade passes City Hall.

storyTitle.en-US: A wall between neighbours on Cupar Way

storyDescription.en-US: A short documentary on one of Belfast’s peace walls, the barriers built between Catholic and Protestant streets during the Troubles. The tallest, on Cupar Way between the Shankill and the Falls, is covered in messages from visitors.

storyTitle.en-US: Families on the decks of Divis Flats, 1980

storyDescription.en-US: A 1980 report from the BBC’s Nationwide magazine show hears from tenants of Divis Flats, the damp, overcrowded 1960s deck-access estate in west Belfast. All but Divis Tower was demolished in the 1990s.

storyTitle.en-US: A night at the most bombed hotel, 1973

storyDescription.en-US: BBC Nationwide spends a night in 1973 at the Europa Hotel on Great Victoria Street, opened in 1971 and bombed again and again during the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland. It was home to the visiting press corps.

storyTitle.en-US: The narrow lanes of the old town

storyDescription.en-US: Local history channel Document Belfast walks the entries, the narrow alleys running off High Street in the old town, such as Pottinger’s Entry and Winecellar Entry, home to some of the city’s oldest pubs.

storyTitle.en-US: Snugs, tiles and gaslight in a Victorian pub

storyDescription.en-US: Document Belfast looks round the Crown Liquor Saloon, a Victorian gin palace on Great Victoria Street with stained glass, mosaic tiles and carved wooden snugs, owned by the National Trust and still a working pub.

locationName.en-US: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street

storyTitle.en-US: The house of endless books where Narnia began

storyDescription.en-US: Lewis scholar Jason Lepojärvi reads from C. S. Lewis’s memoir Surprised by Joy at Little Lea, the east Belfast house the family moved into in 1905, whose rooms of books and attic games fed the boy who later wrote Narnia.

storyTitle.en-US: Inside the white parliament on the hill

storyDescription.en-US: The Northern Ireland Assembly’s own tour of Parliament Buildings at Stormont, the Portland stone parliament opened in 1932 at the top of a mile-long avenue in east Belfast, now home to the devolved Northern Ireland Assembly.

storyTitle.en-US: Exploring Belfast’s Titanic Quarter

storyDescription.en-US: A maritime-heritage walk through the old shipyard district, starting at the marina in Abercorn Basin and passing the restored lighthouse lens known as the Great Light on the way into the land where the Titanic was built.

storyTitle.en-US: Belfast’s Peace Walls Walking Tour: From Divis Tower to Bobby Sands

storyDescription.en-US: A Troubles-history walk through west Belfast, starting at a 1960s tower block once used as an army lookout, following the tall barrier between Catholic and Protestant streets and ending at the mural of a republican hunger striker.

storyTitle.en-US: Boom, Bloodshed, and Belfast’s Remarkable Comeback: A Walking Tour

storyDescription.en-US: Belfast from Victorian industrial boomtown through the Troubles to today, via the Crown Bar, City Hall and the Grand Opera House.

locationName.en-US: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street

storyTitle.en-US: Belfast’s Maritime Mile: A Walking Tour from City Center to Titanic

storyDescription.en-US: Along the river from the old Custom House to the Titanic Quarter, past the docks, cranes and slipways of the city’s shipbuilding past.

storyTitle.en-US: The Heart of Belfast: From Humble Beginnings to Shipbuilding Glory

storyDescription.en-US: How a small market town on the Lagan grew into one of the world’s great shipbuilding and linen cities, told through the streets of the centre.

storyTitle.en-US: Redburn: His First Voyage

storyDescription.en-US: Herman Melville’s half-autobiographical novel of a boy sailor’s first voyage, drawn from his own 1839 trip to Liverpool. The Liverpool chapters show docks, beggars and emigrant ships. His ship ties up at Prince’s Dock, north of the Pier Head.

storyTitle.en-US: The Slave Ship: A Human History

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Marcus Rediker on the ships that carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, built from sailors’ and captives’ own accounts. Liverpool sent more slaving voyages than any other British port. The Town Hall’s frieze includes carved African heads.

storyTitle.en-US: Dead Wake

storyDescription.en-US: Erik Larson on the Cunard liner Lusitania, torpedoed off Ireland in May 1915 with nearly 1,200 dead. She was bound from New York for Liverpool, her home port. Cunard ran its fleet from the Cunard Building on the Pier Head waterfront.

storyTitle.en-US: Twopence to Cross the Mersey

storyDescription.en-US: Helen Forrester’s memoir of a family gone bankrupt and dropped into the slums of 1930s Liverpool. She was kept home from school to mind her six siblings. The title is the ferry fare back to the Wirral. The boats land at Woodside terminal in Birkenhead.

storyTitle.en-US: An Awfully Big Adventure

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist Beryl Bainbridge worked as a teenage stagehand at the Liverpool Playhouse and drew on it for this dark comic novel. A stagestruck girl joins a repertory company in the bomb-damaged city of 1950. The theatre still stands on Williamson Square.

storyTitle.en-US: Tune In: The Beatles: All These Years, Volume 1

storyDescription.en-US: Beatles historian Mark Lewisohn on the band up to the end of 1962, nearly all of it in Liverpool. It’s long. John Lennon met Paul McCartney at a church fête at St Peter’s in Woolton, a village suburb, on 6 July 1957.

storyTitle.en-US: The Mersey Sound

storyDescription.en-US: Penguin’s 1967 collection of three Liverpool poets: painter Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten. Funny, sad, plain-spoken poems about love, pubs and the city. Their patch was Hope Street, which runs between the city’s two cathedrals.

creatorName.en-US: Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten

storyTitle.en-US: Red or Dead

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist David Peace retells Bill Shankly’s fifteen years managing Liverpool FC from 1959, in a deliberately repetitive, chant-like style. It’s long, over 700 pages. Shankly’s bronze statue stands outside Anfield, the club’s stadium, by the Kop stand.

storyTitle.en-US: Liverpool: Wondrous Place

storyDescription.en-US: Music writer Paul Du Noyer, a Liverpudlian, tells the city’s music story from sea shanties and the Beatles to punk and the Cream nightclub. The Cavern Club on Mathew Street is a rebuild. The original cellar was filled in in 1973.

storyTitle.en-US: Hillsborough: The Truth

storyDescription.en-US: Criminologist Phil Scraton on the 1989 crush at Sheffield’s Hillsborough stadium, where 97 Liverpool fans died, and the police cover-up that followed. His work fed the 2012 inquiry. Crowds held a vigil at St George’s Hall, the civic hall, when it reported.

storyTitle.en-US: Distant Voices, Still Lives

storyDescription.en-US: Director Terence Davies’s memory film of his own family in working-class Liverpool in the 1940s and 50s: a violent father, a patient mother, songs sung in pubs. It is slow. Davies grew up in Kensington, an inner-city district east of the centre.

storyTitle.en-US: Nowhere Boy

storyDescription.en-US: Teenage John Lennon caught between his strict Aunt Mimi and his lively mother Julia, until Julia was killed by a car in 1958. Mimi’s house, Mendips on Menlove Avenue, now belongs to the National Trust and can be visited on tours.

storyTitle.en-US: Good Ol’ Freda

storyDescription.en-US: Freda Kelly was 17 when she became the Beatles’ secretary and ran their fan club for over a decade. Then she stayed in Liverpool, worked as a typist and said almost nothing for fifty years. She first saw them at the Cavern Club.

storyTitle.en-US: Of Time and the City

storyDescription.en-US: Terence Davies’s documentary about the Liverpool he grew up in and left, cut from archive film under his own spoken commentary, fond and bitter by turns. The Museum of Liverpool keeps a carriage from the Overhead Railway, the elevated dock line seen in it.

storyTitle.en-US: Boys from the Blackstuff

storyDescription.en-US: Writer Alan Bleasdale’s five-part BBC drama about out-of-work tarmac layers in early-1980s Liverpool. Yosser Hughes’s plea “Gizza job” became a national catchphrase. The Royal Albert Dock, now museums and shops, was derelict when they filmed there.

storyTitle.en-US: Letter to Brezhnev

storyDescription.en-US: Two young women from Kirkby, a 1950s overspill town just outside Liverpool, meet Soviet sailors on a night out, and one writes to Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev to get back to hers. Written by Frank Clarke and made on a tiny budget.

storyTitle.en-US: Brookside

storyDescription.en-US: Producer Phil Redmond’s soap opera launched with Channel 4 in 1982 and ran 21 years. It was shot in real houses on a new cul-de-sac in Croxteth Park, a suburban estate, and took on strikes, drugs and unemployment.

storyTitle.en-US: Hillsborough

storyDescription.en-US: Daniel Gordon’s documentary on the 1989 Hillsborough stadium crush in Sheffield and the families’ long fight to overturn the police version of events. The memorial to the dead stands beside Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium.

storyTitle.en-US: Violent Playground

storyDescription.en-US: Director Basil Dearden’s drama about a Liverpool policeman, played by Stanley Baker, moved to youth work and up against a teenage arsonist played by David McCallum. It was shot around Gerard Gardens, inner-city council tenements since demolished.

storyTitle.en-US: Dockers

storyDescription.en-US: Television film about the Liverpool dock strike of 1995–98, when some 500 dockers were sacked after refusing to cross a picket line. Writers Jimmy McGovern and Irvine Welsh made it with the sacked men, whose pickets stood at the Royal Seaforth Dock gates.

storyTitle.en-US: Bread
