storyDescription.en-US: Writer Carla Lane’s BBC sitcom, 1986–91, about the Boswells, a big Catholic family in the Dingle, a working-class district by the south docks, getting by on the dole and small scams in Thatcher’s Britain, all under their mother Nellie’s rule.

storyTitle.en-US: You’ll Never Walk Alone

storyDescription.en-US: Gerry Marsden’s band took this show tune from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s musical “Carousel” to No. 1 in 1963. Fans on the Kop, the home end at Liverpool FC’s Anfield stadium, adopted it as their anthem, and it is still sung before every home match.

storyTitle.en-US: Anyone Who Had a Heart

storyDescription.en-US: Cilla Black worked the cloakroom at the Cavern Club, the Mathew Street cellar where the Beatles played, before Brian Epstein signed her. Her version of this Burt Bacharach song went to No. 1 in 1964; a statue of her now stands outside the club.

storyTitle.en-US: Ferry Cross the Mersey

storyDescription.en-US: Gerry Marsden wrote this for the 1964 film of the same name, about the boats linking Liverpool and Birkenhead. The Mersey Ferries still leave from the Pier Head terminal, and the song plays on board as they cross the river.

storyTitle.en-US: Penny Lane

storyDescription.en-US: Paul McCartney’s picture of the street and bus terminus near where he and John Lennon grew up: the barber, the bank, the fireman and the “shelter in the middle of the roundabout,” which still stands at Smithdown Place by Penny Lane.

storyTitle.en-US: Strawberry Fields Forever

storyDescription.en-US: John Lennon grew up near Strawberry Field, a Salvation Army children’s home in Woolton, and played in its garden as a boy. The red gates are a pilgrimage spot, and the site now has a visitor centre about the home and the song.

storyTitle.en-US: Maggie Mae

storyDescription.en-US: A 40-second scrap of an old Liverpool sailors’ song on the Beatles’ “Let It Be,” about a woman who robbed a sailor “down Lime Street.” The street runs past Lime Street station, the city’s main railway terminus, and St George’s Hall.

storyTitle.en-US: Children of the Ghetto

storyDescription.en-US: Brothers Chris and Eddie Amoo of the Real Thing, Britain’s first Black chart-topping band, wrote this about their own district, Liverpool 8, or Toxteth. Granby Street was the heart of its Black community, one of the oldest in Britain.

storyTitle.en-US: Electricity

storyDescription.en-US: Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys, teenagers from Meols on the Wirral peninsula across the Mersey from Liverpool, formed OMD in 1978. This debut single, about wasted energy, came out on Manchester’s Factory Records in 1979.

storyTitle.en-US: Relax

storyDescription.en-US: Singer Holly Johnson came out of the punk scene at Eric’s, the late-1970s club opposite the Cavern on Mathew Street. His band Frankie Goes to Hollywood’s debut was banned by BBC Radio 1 in 1984 and became one of Britain’s best-selling singles.

locationName.en-US: Site of Eric’s club, Mathew Street

storyTitle.en-US: The Killing Moon

storyDescription.en-US: Ian McCulloch’s band Echo & the Bunnymen grew out of Liverpool’s post-punk scene; In May 1984 they led fans on “A Crystal Day” around the city, ending with a concert in St George’s Hall, the columned concert hall on Lime Street.

storyTitle.en-US: All Together Now

storyDescription.en-US: Peter Hooton’s band the Farm set the 1914 Christmas truce, when British and German soldiers stopped fighting, to Pachelbel’s Canon. A statue of the truce football match stands in St Luke’s, a church gutted in the 1941 Blitz and left roofless.

storyTitle.en-US: Dreaming of You

storyDescription.en-US: The Coral formed in Hoylake, a seaside town at the tip of the Wirral peninsula, as teenagers in the 1990s. This short, Merseybeat-tinged single from their 2002 debut album is the song most people know them by.

storyTitle.en-US: Let’s Dance to Joy Division

storyDescription.en-US: The Wombats met as students at LIPA, the performing arts school co-founded by Paul McCartney in his old school building on Mount Street. Matthew Murphy’s song is about dancing badly to the Manchester post-punk band Joy Division.

storyTitle.en-US: The world’s first commercial wet dock, buried under a shopping centre

storyDescription.en-US: Thomas Steers’s Old Dock opened in 1715 as the world’s first enclosed commercial wet dock, was filled in during the 1820s and rediscovered in 2001 beneath what is now the Liverpool ONE shopping district. National Museums Liverpool tells its story.

storyTitle.en-US: The port that made Liverpool, and the warehouses built not to burn

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Dan Snow on Liverpool’s docks, which made it Britain’s great Atlantic port. Their showpiece is the Royal Albert Dock, Jesse Hartley’s 1846 ring of iron, brick and stone warehouses built so that nothing in them could catch fire.

storyTitle.en-US: How a city remembers the trade that built its wealth

storyDescription.en-US: By the late 1700s Liverpool was Britain’s leading slaving port. This episode looks at how the city has come to remember that past, including the International Slavery Museum, opened on the waterfront in 2007 for the bicentenary of abolition.

locationName.en-US: International Slavery Museum, Royal Albert Dock

storyTitle.en-US: Four Liverpool teenagers and the cellar club where it started

storyDescription.en-US: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook on the Beatles, who played the Cavern Club, a cellar club on Mathew Street, close to 300 times in 1961–63. The original cellar was filled in in 1973; today’s club is a rebuilt version a few yards away.

storyTitle.en-US: Ninety-seven fans, a cover-up and a city’s long fight for the truth

storyDescription.en-US: Lindsay Graham recounts the 1989 FA Cup semi-final crush at Sheffield’s Hillsborough stadium that killed 97 Liverpool fans, and the police smears that followed. Inquests in 2016 found they were unlawfully killed. Their memorial stands at Anfield stadium.

storyTitle.en-US: A Cunard liner torpedoed on its way home to Liverpool

storyDescription.en-US: On 7 May 1915 a German U-boat sank the Cunard liner Lusitania off Ireland as it sailed from New York to Liverpool; about 1,200 died. Witness History draws on archive survivor accounts. Cunard’s old headquarters, the Cunard Building, stands at Pier Head.

storyTitle.en-US: Wartime sailors deported, families left behind

storyDescription.en-US: Thousands of Chinese seamen kept supplies reaching Liverpool in the Second World War. After 1945 the British authorities forced many out, leaving wives and children behind. Many sailed for the Blue Funnel Line, based at India Buildings on Water Street.

storyTitle.en-US: The first intercity railway nearly dies in Parliament

storyDescription.en-US: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway of 1830 was the first intercity line worked only by steam, yet engineer George Stephenson nearly sank it in Parliament. Its Liverpool end climbed to Edge Hill, where the 1836 station still takes passengers.

storyTitle.en-US: A concrete tent under a stained-glass crown

storyDescription.en-US: Writer David Trigg and Laura Moffatt of Art + Christianity tour the art of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King, England’s largest Catholic cathedral, a circular 1967 church under John Piper’s glass lantern, with former organist Terry Duffy.

locationName.en-US: Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King

storyTitle.en-US: Britain’s biggest cathedral, raised over an old quarry

storyDescription.en-US: Uncharted Liverpool on the Anglican Liverpool Cathedral: why it was built on St James’s Mount, above a former quarry turned cemetery, who designed it, and the odd details inside. Begun in 1904 and finished in 1978, it is Britain’s largest cathedral.

storyTitle.en-US: The women who worked the sugar refinery on Love Lane

storyDescription.en-US: Authors Duncan Barrett and Nuala Calvi on The Sugar Girls of Love Lane, their book of stories from women who worked at Tate & Lyle’s sugar refinery on Love Lane, in the dockside Vauxhall district, in the 1960s. The refinery closed in 1981.

locationName.en-US: Tate & Lyle refinery site, Love Lane

storyTitle.en-US: Bombs, rumours and the government’s morale reports

storyDescription.en-US: A talk from The National Archives on how the wartime government measured the morale of Liverpudlians during the Blitz, some of the heaviest bombing in Britain. St Luke’s Church, burned out in May 1941, stands roofless on Leece Street as a memorial.

locationName.en-US: St Luke’s bombed-out church, Leece Street

storyTitle.en-US: How a port city came to talk Scouse

storyDescription.en-US: Linguist Tony Crowley, who grew up in central Liverpool, on Scouse, the city’s accent and dialect, named after lobscouse, a sailors’ stew. Scotland Road, the old Irish working-class district north of the centre, is where much of that mix of voices settled.

storyTitle.en-US: A seventieth birthday on the Mersey ferry

storyDescription.en-US: Liverpool-born politician and novelist Edwina Currie, who turned 70 the same year as BBC Radio 3, marks its birthday with an essay on the ferry across the River Mersey, which sails from the Pier Head terminal.

storyTitle.en-US: A church fête, a skiffle band and a boy with a guitar

storyDescription.en-US: On 6 July 1957 John Lennon’s skiffle group the Quarrymen played the summer fête at St Peter’s Church in Woolton, a south Liverpool suburb. That afternoon a friend introduced him to 15-year-old Paul McCartney. The Retrospectors tell the story.

stories.__channel: Today In History with The Retrospectors
stories.__iconKey: Today In History with The Retrospectors

storyTitle.en-US: A radical city and its fight with Westminster

storyDescription.en-US: Historian David Swift, author of Scouse Republic, on Liverpool’s radical politics and its 1980s decline, when the Labour council, run from the Municipal Buildings on Dale Street, defied Margaret Thatcher’s government over its budget.

storyTitle.en-US: Thirty years of digging, and no reason given

storyDescription.en-US: Tobacco merchant Joseph Williamson paid men for about 30 years to dig tunnels under his Edge Hill estate and never said why. Jimmy Akin and Dom Bettinelli weigh seven theories. Part of the maze is open at the Williamson Tunnels Heritage Centre.

locationName.en-US: Williamson Tunnels Heritage Centre, Smithdown Lane

storyTitle.en-US: Liverpool’s slave-trade past, read in its streets and stones

storyDescription.en-US: Liverpool ships carried well over a million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Behind the Town Hall, the merchants’ square of Exchange Flags holds the 1813 Nelson monument, whose four chained captives are often read as an echo of that trade.

storyTitle.en-US: A museum on the dock where slaving ships were fitted out

storyDescription.en-US: An introduction to the International Slavery Museum, opened in 2007 inside the Merseyside Maritime Museum on the Royal Albert Dock. It covers the transatlantic slave trade, Liverpool’s central part in it, and racism and resistance since.

locationName.en-US: International Slavery Museum, Royal Albert Dock

storyTitle.en-US: Twenty-two-year-old architect, seventy-four years of building

storyDescription.en-US: Architect Giles Gilbert Scott won the competition for Liverpool’s Anglican cathedral in 1903, aged 22. Building ran from 1904 to 1978, long after his death, producing Britain’s largest cathedral on a sandstone ridge above the city.

storyTitle.en-US: Concrete, clock towers and two copper birds

storyDescription.en-US: Walter Aubrey Thomas’s Royal Liver Building, finished in 1911 for an insurance society, was among the first big reinforced-concrete buildings. Its two Liver Birds, the city’s mythical emblem, watch over the Pier Head waterfront and the river.

storyTitle.en-US: Europe’s oldest Chinese community, filmed in 1981

storyDescription.en-US: Archive footage of Liverpool’s Chinatown, home to Europe’s oldest Chinese community, which grew from seamen of the Blue Funnel shipping line in the late 1800s. Its centre is Nelson Street, now marked by a large ornamental arch built in 2000.

storyTitle.en-US: The Chinese seamen shipped out of Liverpool after the war

storyDescription.en-US: In 1945–46 the British government quietly deported hundreds of Chinese merchant seamen from Liverpool, many leaving wives and children who never learned why. A plaque on the Pier Head waterfront has remembered them since 2006.

locationName.en-US: Chinese seamen memorial plaque, Pier Head

storyTitle.en-US: Granada’s current-affairs cameras return to Toxteth

storyDescription.en-US: Granada TV’s World in Action returns to Toxteth, the inner-city district where July 1981 saw days of rioting between young people and police after an arrest. Upper Parliament Street, where the Rialto ballroom burned, was at its centre.

storyTitle.en-US: Toxteth’s 1981 riots, told from inside the neighbourhood

storyDescription.en-US: The 1981 Toxteth riots as seen from L8, the postcode of Liverpool’s long-established Black community. Granby Street, the district’s old shopping street, was at the heart of the area worst affected by the unrest and the neglect that followed.

storyTitle.en-US: A swaying wall of singing on the Anfield terrace

storyDescription.en-US: A 1974 BBC film on the Kop, the vast standing terrace behind one goal at Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium, named after Spion Kop, a Boer War hill. Its crowd swayed and sang as one. The terrace became all-seated in 1994.

storyTitle.en-US: Everton fans tell their own club’s story

storyDescription.en-US: Everton supporters tell the history of their club, founded by a Methodist chapel side in 1878. From 1892 Everton played at Goodison Park in Walton, one of the oldest purpose-built football grounds, before moving to Bramley-Moore Dock in 2025.

storyTitle.en-US: An electric railway on stilts along the docks

storyDescription.en-US: Rail historian Ruairidh MacVeigh on the Liverpool Overhead Railway, an electric elevated line opened in 1893 above the Dock Road, past docks such as Stanley Dock. Known as the dockers’ umbrella, it closed in 1956 and was pulled down soon after.

storyTitle.en-US: A temple for concerts and courts opposite Lime Street

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Steve Binns on St George’s Hall, the neoclassical concert hall and law courts of 1854 opposite Lime Street station. Its young architect, Harvey Lonsdale Elmes, died before it was finished; its floor of some 30,000 Minton tiles is usually covered.

storyTitle.en-US: Victorian painters who rejected the art academy

storyDescription.en-US: National Museums Liverpool introduces the Pre-Raphaelites, the Victorian painters around Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt. The Walker Art Gallery on William Brown Street has one of the major collections of their work.

storyTitle.en-US: The cathedral that would have outdomed St Peter’s

storyDescription.en-US: Architect Edwin Lutyens designed a Catholic cathedral for Liverpool with a dome larger than St Peter’s in Rome. Work began in 1933 and halted with the war; only the brick and granite crypt was built, and the 1967 cathedral now sits on top of it.

storyTitle.en-US: Hidden Histories: Liverpool’s Links to the Transatlantic Slave Trade

storyDescription.en-US: A walk through the buildings and street names of central Liverpool that still carry the city’s ties to the transatlantic slave trade, which made its 18th-century fortune.

storyTitle.en-US: The Beatles, Docks and Rock ’n’ Roll: Liverpool’s Musical Heritage

storyDescription.en-US: From the Albert Dock along the waterfront to the Cavern Club on Mathew Street, mixing Beatles history with the story of the port that shaped the city.

storyTitle.en-US: It Wisnae Us: The Truth About Glasgow and Slavery

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Stephen Mullen’s short guide to how Atlantic slavery paid for the city centre. Tobacco lord William Cunninghame built a mansion in 1778 off Queen Street. It is now the Gallery of Modern Art. The title is Scots for “it wasn’t us.”

locationName.en-US: Gallery of Modern Art, Royal Exchange Square

storyTitle.en-US: Charles Rennie Mackintosh

storyDescription.en-US: Architectural historian Alan Crawford’s compact illustrated life of Glasgow’s great architect and designer. His masterpiece was the Glasgow School of Art building on Renfrew Street. It burned in 2014 and again in 2018. Restoration is still under way.

locationName.en-US: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building

storyTitle.en-US: Tea and Taste: The Glasgow Tea Rooms 1875–1975

storyDescription.en-US: Design historian Perilla Kinchin on how Glasgow, a city of temperance campaigners, built a tea-room culture. Businesswoman Kate Cranston hired Mackintosh to design the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street in 1903. You can still have tea there.

locationName.en-US: Willow Tea Rooms building, Sauchiehall Street

storyTitle.en-US: When the Clyde Ran Red: A Social History of Red Clydeside

storyDescription.en-US: Historian Maggie Craig on Red Clydeside, the strikes and protests of 1910–1922. In 1915 Govan housewife Mary Barbour led a rent strike that forced a national rent freeze. Her statue has stood at Govan Cross, the old town square, since 2018.

storyTitle.en-US: Growing Up in the Gorbals

storyDescription.en-US: Ralph Glasser’s memoir of a poor Jewish childhood in the Gorbals tenements, south of the river, in the 1920s and ’30s. He worked in a barber’s and a garment factory, won a place at Oxford, and cycled there. The tenements were cleared in the 1960s.

storyTitle.en-US: Lanark

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist and painter Alasdair Gray’s novel, half realist, half fantasy. Its hero, art student Duncan Thaw, grows up in Riddrie, the east-end council estate where Gray grew up. It argues that Glasgow needs artists to imagine it. It’s long.

storyTitle.en-US: Windswept & Interesting

storyDescription.en-US: Comedian Billy Connolly’s memoir of a hard Glasgow boyhood and how he found his voice. Before folk music and stand-up he was a welder at Alexander Stephen & Sons, a shipyard at Linthouse on the Clyde. The yard closed in 1968. It is very funny.

locationName.en-US: Site of Alexander Stephen & Sons shipyard, Linthouse

storyTitle.en-US: New Selected Poems

storyDescription.en-US: Poems by Edwin Morgan, Glasgow’s first poet laureate and later Scotland’s national poet. He wrote about the city for sixty years: tenements, demolitions, a Glasgow Green park poem about men meeting in the dark. He came out publicly at seventy.

storyTitle.en-US: Jock Stein: The Definitive Biography

storyDescription.en-US: Broadcaster Archie Macpherson’s life of the former miner who managed Celtic Football Club. In 1967 his team, all born near Glasgow, became the first British side to win the European Cup. Their ground is Celtic Park, the stadium in Parkhead.

storyTitle.en-US: Laidlaw

storyDescription.en-US: Novelist William McIlvanney’s first Glasgow detective story, often called the start of Scottish crime writing known as Tartan Noir. A girl is found murdered in Kelvingrove Park, the Victorian park in the West End. The city’s pubs and streets do the rest.

storyTitle.en-US: Shuggie Bain

storyDescription.en-US: Douglas Stuart’s Booker Prize-winning novel about a boy and his alcoholic mother in 1980s Glasgow, as the shipyards and pits closed. It begins in the Sighthill tower blocks north of the centre. The towers were demolished in 2016. Stuart grew up there.

storyTitle.en-US: Small Faces

storyDescription.en-US: Director Gillies MacKinnon’s drama about three teenage brothers caught up in the street gangs of 1968 Glasgow. One wants to be an artist. A key scene plays out in Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the red sandstone museum in the West End.

storyTitle.en-US: Ratcatcher

storyDescription.en-US: Lynne Ramsay’s first feature: a boy in a tenement during the 1973 binmen’s strike, when rubbish piled up across the city. Slow and quiet. The canal at its centre is the Forth and Clyde, which runs through Maryhill in the north of the city.

storyTitle.en-US: Taggart

storyDescription.en-US: Writer Glenn Chandler’s Glasgow murder series ran for 27 years, set around Maryhill police station. “There’s been a murder” became a catchphrase. The Glasgow Necropolis, the Victorian hilltop cemetery behind the cathedral, was a favourite location.

storyTitle.en-US: Comfort and Joy

storyDescription.en-US: Director Bill Forsyth’s comedy about a radio DJ caught between rival ice-cream van firms. It came out just as Glasgow’s real ice-cream wars turned deadly: six of the Doyle family died in an arson attack on their Ruchazie flat in April 1984.

storyTitle.en-US: My Name Is Joe

storyDescription.en-US: Ken Loach’s drama about a recovering alcoholic coaching a boys’ football team and falling for a health visitor. Peter Mullan won Best Actor at Cannes. It was shot in Ruchill, a north Glasgow district, with local non-actors. The dialect is thick.

storyTitle.en-US: Still Game

storyDescription.en-US: Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill’s sitcom about two pensioners, Jack and Victor, in a tower block in a fictional Glasgow scheme. It ran on and off until 2019. Live stage versions sold out the Hydro, the big arena by the Clyde, for weeks.

storyTitle.en-US: Red Road

storyDescription.en-US: Andrea Arnold’s first feature. A CCTV operator watching the city on screens spots a man from her past. Much of it unfolds in the Red Road flats, once among Europe’s tallest housing blocks. They were demolished between 2012 and 2015.

locationName.en-US: Site of the Red Road flats

storyTitle.en-US: Under the Skin

storyDescription.en-US: Jonathan Glazer’s science-fiction film with Scarlett Johansson as an alien driving a van, picking up men. Many street scenes were shot with hidden cameras on real shoppers on Argyle Street, the city’s main shopping street. Strange and slow.

storyTitle.en-US: Rab C. Nesbitt

storyDescription.en-US: Writer Ian Pattison’s BBC Scotland sitcom about Rab C. Nesbitt, an unemployed street philosopher in a string vest, played by Gregor Fisher, and his family in Govan, the old shipbuilding district on the south bank of the Clyde.

storyTitle.en-US: The Angels’ Share

storyDescription.en-US: Director Ken Loach and writer Paul Laverty’s comedy about Robbie, a young Glaswegian sentenced in the city’s sheriff court to community service, who finds a nose for whisky. The Sheriff Court stands on the south bank of the Clyde in the Gorbals.

storyTitle.en-US: I Belong to Glasgow

storyDescription.en-US: Dundee-born music-hall comedian Will Fyffe said he wrote this tipsy anthem after a cheerful drunk talked to him at Glasgow Central Station. Its chorus, “Glasgow belongs to me,” is still sung in the city’s pubs a century on.

storyTitle.en-US: Rock Island Line

storyDescription.en-US: Lonnie Donegan, the “King of Skiffle,” was born in the East End district of Bridgeton in 1931. His sped-up take on Lead Belly’s railroad song set off a craze for washboards and tea-chest basses that put guitars in the hands of the young Beatles.

storyTitle.en-US: Shout

storyDescription.en-US: Lulu, born Marie Lawrie, was 15 and living in the tenements of Dennistoun in the East End when she belted out this Isley Brothers cover. It went Top 10 in Britain, and she has been closing shows with it ever since.

storyTitle.en-US: The Jeely Piece Song

storyDescription.en-US: A child in a new tower block can’t get a jeely piece (a jam sandwich) thrown down from the 20th floor. Folk singer Adam McNaughtan’s comic protest about the 1960s high-rises is pinned here at the site of the Red Road flats, demolished in 2015.

storyTitle.en-US: Delilah

storyDescription.en-US: Rock showman Alex Harvey grew up in the Gorbals, the tenement district on the south bank of the Clyde. His band turned Tom Jones’s murder ballad into a stomping piece of theatre, and their live recording reached the UK Top 10.

storyTitle.en-US: Blue Boy

storyDescription.en-US: Edwyn Collins’s band made this jangling single for Postcard Records, run by Alan Horne from a tenement flat on West Princes Street. Postcard’s “Sound of Young Scotland” gave British indie music a template for the decade.

storyTitle.en-US: Waterfront

storyDescription.en-US: Jim Kerr’s band sing about the Clyde riverside on this bass-driven anthem, and filmed its video at the Barrowland Ballroom, the old East End dance hall that became the city’s favourite rock venue.

storyTitle.en-US: Tinseltown in the Rain

storyDescription.en-US: Paul Buchanan and Robert Bell met as students at the University of Glasgow before forming The Blue Nile. This string-swept single from “A Walk Across the Rooftops” turns a wet night in the city into something cinematic.

storyTitle.en-US: Dignity

storyDescription.en-US: Ricky Ross’s band sing about a council road sweeper saving up to buy a little boat he’ll call Dignity. It is pinned at the City Chambers on George Square, the grand Victorian headquarters of the council he works for.

storyTitle.en-US: The Concept

storyDescription.en-US: Teenage Fanclub came out of Bellshill, a town on Glasgow’s eastern edge whose 1980s guitar scene became known as “the Bellshill Sound.” This six-minute opener of “Bandwagonesque” fades out on a long, harmony-laden coda.

storyTitle.en-US: The State I Am In

storyDescription.en-US: Stuart Murdoch’s band recorded their first album, “Tigermilk,” as a project for the Electric Honey label run by music students at Stow College. This wry, confessional opener began a cult that grew well beyond Glasgow.

storyTitle.en-US: Why Does It Always Rain on Me?

storyDescription.en-US: Singer Fran Healy was an art student at the Glasgow School of Art, Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s building on Renfrew Street, when Travis took shape. This rueful hit about bad luck and grey skies made them one of Britain’s biggest bands.

storyTitle.en-US: Take Me Out

storyDescription.en-US: Before Franz Ferdinand, Alex Kapranos booked bands at the 13th Note, a vegetarian café and basement venue on King Street. The band’s tempo-shifting breakthrough single was nominated for a Grammy and took Glasgow art-rock worldwide.

storyTitle.en-US: Geraldine

storyDescription.en-US: Glasvegas come from Dalmarnock, an East End district by the Clyde. Singer James Allan wrote this wall-of-sound ballad in the voice of a social worker, and sings it in his own unvarnished Glasgow accent.

storyTitle.en-US: The Mother We Share

storyDescription.en-US: Glasgow synth-pop trio CHVRCHES, led by singer Lauren Mayberry, a law graduate of the University of Strathclyde, broke out with this bright, glassy debut single. It set up a career of stadium tours and festival headlines.

storyTitle.en-US: Tobacco fortunes and the streets they built

storyDescription.en-US: Historian and broadcaster Neil Oliver on Glasgow’s 18th-century tobacco lords, whose wealth came from plantations worked by enslaved people, and on the Merchant City, the quarter of streets and mansions they built east of George Square.

storyTitle.en-US: Saint, cathedral, trading port, workshop of the Empire

storyDescription.en-US: A one-episode history of Glasgow, which grew up around the medieval cathedral of St Mungo, the city’s patron saint, and became a transatlantic trading port and then one of the world’s great shipbuilding and engineering cities.

storyTitle.en-US: Sixty-six fans die on a stairway after a New Year derby

storyDescription.en-US: On 2 January 1971, as fans left the Old Firm derby between Glasgow’s two big clubs, Rangers and Celtic, a crush on Stairway 13 at Ibrox Stadium killed 66 people. The disaster led to Britain’s first stadium safety law in 1975.

storyTitle.en-US: Art therapy for the most violent men in Scotland’s prisons

storyDescription.en-US: In 1973 the Special Unit at Barlinnie Prison, Glasgow’s Victorian jail in Riddrie, began giving violent long-term prisoners art materials and a say in their own regime. Its best-known inmate, gangster Jimmy Boyle, left as a sculptor.

storyTitle.en-US: Shipyard workers refuse to let their yards close

storyDescription.en-US: In 1971 the government let Upper Clyde Shipbuilders fail. Led by shop stewards Jimmy Reid and Jimmy Airlie, workers kept building ships instead of striking. One of the yards was Fairfield in Govan, whose 1890s offices still face Govan Road.

storyTitle.en-US: Tanks in the city after a riot in the main square

storyDescription.en-US: Versus History talks to writer Donny O’Rourke about 31 January 1919, when police charged strikers campaigning for a 40-hour week in George Square, Glasgow’s civic square. The government sent troops, and tanks waited in the cattle market.

storyTitle.en-US: The art school that burned twice

storyDescription.en-US: Cultural historian Robyne Calvert on architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh and his Glasgow School of Art on Renfrew Street, finished in 1909 and gutted by fires in 2014 and 2018.

locationName.en-US: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building

storyTitle.en-US: The wife Mackintosh said was three-quarters of his work

storyDescription.en-US: The National Trust for Scotland’s podcast on artist Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh, wife and collaborator of Charles Rennie Mackintosh. The Hunterian Art Gallery at the University of Glasgow has rebuilt the interiors of the couple’s home.

locationName.en-US: The Mackintosh House, Hunterian Art Gallery

storyTitle.en-US: A dance hall built by a market queen

storyDescription.en-US: Writer Alison Irvine on the Barrowland Ballroom on the Gallowgate, opened on Christmas Eve 1934 by market trader Maggie McIver as an East End dance hall. Its neon sign and sprung floor later made it one of Britain’s best-loved rock venues.

storyTitle.en-US: How Glasgow taught the world to pass

storyDescription.en-US: Richard McBrearty of the Scottish Football Museum at Hampden Park, Scotland’s national stadium, on early Glasgow football: Queen’s Park, the amateur club that pioneered the passing game, and the Irish community clubs that followed.

storyTitle.en-US: Photographing the slums before the demolition crews

storyDescription.en-US: Glasgow’s Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons on photographer Thomas Annan, hired in 1868 to record the closes, narrow alleys off the Saltmarket and High Street, before the city cleared them: some of the first photographs of slum housing.

storyTitle.en-US: A modernist world’s fair in a south side park

storyDescription.en-US: This Day in Scottish History recalls the 1938 Empire Exhibition in Bellahouston Park, south of the Clyde, which drew nearly 13 million visitors to its modernist pavilions and 300-foot Tait Tower. The Palace of Art is one of the few buildings left.

storyTitle.en-US: The novelist who painted the city’s ceilings

storyDescription.en-US: Sorcha Dallas, custodian of the Alasdair Gray Archive, on the Glasgow writer and artist behind the novel Lanark. His murals are all over the city; the largest is the starry ceiling of Òran Mór, a former church turned arts venue on Byres Road.

storyTitle.en-US: A ship launched with its builders aboard

storyDescription.en-US: In July 1883 the steamer Daphne capsized moments after launch at Alexander Stephen’s Linthouse yard on the Clyde, drowning 124 of the shipyard workers still aboard. Scottish History Out of Order visits their graves in Craigton Cemetery.

storyTitle.en-US: The speech the New York Times compared to Gettysburg

storyDescription.en-US: Former Scottish justice secretary Kenny MacAskill on “A rat race is for rats”, the 1972 address by shipyard union leader Jimmy Reid on becoming rector of the University of Glasgow. The New York Times printed it in full.

storyTitle.en-US: From the Gorbals to guarding Abraham Lincoln

storyDescription.en-US: Actor Alex Norton narrates the story of Allan Pinkerton, born in 1819 in the Gorbals, the old tenement district south of the river, who emigrated to the US, foiled a plot against Abraham Lincoln and founded the Pinkerton detective agency.

storyTitle.en-US: Hundreds of children hunt a vampire in a graveyard

storyDescription.en-US: One night in 1954 hundreds of Gorbals children armed with knives and stakes stormed the Southern Necropolis, a Victorian cemetery, hunting an iron-toothed vampire. The Hebejeebies podcast asks how the rumour started and who got blamed.

storyTitle.en-US: Suffragette bodyguards against the Glasgow police

storyDescription.en-US: In March 1914 police stormed the stage at St Andrew’s Halls to arrest suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst, and her jiu-jitsu-trained bodyguard fought back. Only the halls’ facade survived a 1962 fire; the Mitchell Library now fills it.

storyTitle.en-US: The restaurant that claims chicken tikka masala

storyDescription.en-US: The Judge Reviews talks to Asif of the Shish Mahal, the West End curry house whose founder Ali Ahmed Aslam said he invented chicken tikka masala there around 1971 by adding a tomato sauce to dry tandoori chicken for a customer.

storyTitle.en-US: A sandstone palace of art built for an exhibition

storyDescription.en-US: Travel writer Rick Steves visits Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the red sandstone building opened for Glasgow’s 1901 International Exhibition, where free admission puts Salvador Dalí’s Christ of St John of the Cross near a hanging Spitfire.

storyTitle.en-US: The pedestrian spine of the Victorian city centre

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves walks Buchanan Street, Glasgow’s pedestrianised main shopping street, which runs downhill from the Royal Concert Hall to Argyle Street between Victorian sandstone frontages, glass-roofed arcades and street musicians.

storyTitle.en-US: Gable-end murals across the city centre

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves on the giant murals painted on Glasgow’s city-centre gable walls, a trail whose best-known stop is the artist Smug’s modern St Mungo, the city’s patron saint, cradling a robin on High Street.

storyTitle.en-US: The world’s third-oldest underground, still one small circle

storyDescription.en-US: Transport filmmaker Geoff Marshall rides the Glasgow Subway, opened in 1896 after London’s and Budapest’s: one 15-station loop under both banks of the Clyde, with trains small enough to earn the nickname the Clockwork Orange.

storyTitle.en-US: Building the QE2 in the last great Clyde yard

storyDescription.en-US: BBC footage from 1967 of the workers at John Brown & Company in Clydebank, just downriver from Glasgow, building the liner Queen Elizabeth 2. The yard’s giant 1907 Titan crane still stands on the riverbank.

storyTitle.en-US: A museum of ordinary Glaswegian life

storyDescription.en-US: In Glasgow Museums’ Glasgow Histories series, Peter Mortimer tells the story of the People’s Palace, the 1898 red sandstone museum of the city’s social history on Glasgow Green, the oldest park in the city, with a glasshouse Winter Gardens behind.

storyTitle.en-US: Virginia leaf and the merchants who grew rich on it

storyDescription.en-US: A clip from the BBC series Union on how the 1707 union with England opened colonial trade to Glasgow, whose tobacco lords grew rich on leaf grown by enslaved people in Virginia. The 1775 Tobacco Merchant’s House survives on Miller Street.

storyTitle.en-US: Repairing a medieval cathedral the medieval way

storyDescription.en-US: Historic Environment Scotland on conserving Glasgow Cathedral, the 13th-century church on the site of St Mungo’s grave and the only medieval cathedral on the Scottish mainland to come through the 1560 Reformation almost intact.

storyTitle.en-US: A shipowner’s 9,000 objects in a glass-walled park museum

storyDescription.en-US: STV News goes behind the scenes at the Burrell Collection in Pollok Country Park, the art, armour, tapestries and ceramics shipping magnate William Burrell gave the city in 1944, rehoused after a six-year refurbishment that ended in 2022.

storyTitle.en-US: Trams, locomotives and a tall ship on the riverbank

storyDescription.en-US: The Daily Record’s short tour of the Riverside Museum, Glasgow’s transport museum, a zigzag shed by architect Zaha Hadid at the mouth of the River Kelvin. The museum keeps old trams, Clyde-built locomotives and the tall ship Glenlee.

storyTitle.en-US: A tenement flat left as it was in 1965

storyDescription.en-US: Rick Steves visits the Tenement House in Garnethill, where shorthand typist Agnes Toward lived from 1911 to 1965. The National Trust for Scotland keeps her flat as she left it, with gaslight, a coal range and beds built into wall recesses.

storyTitle.en-US: Miss Cranston’s tea rooms, restored

storyDescription.en-US: A Doors Open Days film on the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street, designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh for tea-room owner Kate Cranston and opened in 1903. A trust rescued the building and reopened it in 2018 as Mackintosh at the Willow.

locationName.en-US: Mackintosh at the Willow, Sauchiehall Street

storyTitle.en-US: A hill of Victorian merchants’ monuments

storyDescription.en-US: The volunteer Friends of Glasgow Necropolis show the garden cemetery opened in 1833 on the hill behind the cathedral, where the city’s merchants and industrialists competed in stone under a column topped by reformer John Knox.

storyTitle.en-US: A century of the Barras

storyDescription.en-US: Glasgow Building Preservation Trust marks a hundred years of the Barras, the East End weekend market that Maggie McIver started by renting out barrows, the handcarts that gave it its name, before building the covered market and the Barrowland dance hall.

storyTitle.en-US: Why the Duke wears a traffic cone

storyDescription.en-US: The local history channel Astonishing Glasgow on Carlo Marochetti’s 1844 equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington outside the Gallery of Modern Art, which has worn a traffic cone on its head, put there by late-night climbers, since the 1980s.

locationName.en-US: Duke of Wellington statue, Royal Exchange Square

storyTitle.en-US: The rent strike that beat Glasgow’s landlords

storyDescription.en-US: Scottish History Out Of Order on Mary Barbour, the Govan housewife who in 1915 led tenants against wartime rent rises; the strike forced Parliament to freeze rents. Her statue, leading a crowd of women, stands at Govan Cross.

storyTitle.en-US: The only house left from medieval Glasgow

storyDescription.en-US: STV News on Provan’s Lordship, built in 1471 opposite the cathedral as part of a hospital, the oldest house in Glasgow and one of just four medieval buildings left in the city. It is now a free museum with a physic garden behind it.

storyTitle.en-US: Religion, Ireland and ninety minutes of football

storyDescription.en-US: The Department of Information on the Old Firm, the rivalry between Glasgow’s Celtic and Rangers, rooted in Irish Catholic immigration and Protestant loyalism. Celtic play at Celtic Park in the East End, known locally as Parkhead.

storyTitle.en-US: Glasgow through the ages: A sightseeing walk from the Cathedral to Glasgow Green

storyDescription.en-US: A history walk through the oldest part of Glasgow, starting at the medieval cathedral and the legend of its patron saint, then down the old pilgrims’ high street past a herb garden and history murals, finishing in the city’s oldest public park.

storyTitle.en-US: Glasgow: The Merchant City

storyDescription.en-US: A history of Glasgow’s trade wealth, from tobacco and cotton to heavy engineering and the city’s ties to slavery and abolition, starting in the main civic square and passing a cone-hatted equestrian statue, ending on a Georgian square uphill.

storyTitle.en-US: Ghouls and Gruesome Tales: A Glasgow Ghost tour with Where Now

storyDescription.en-US: Ghost stories and grim history told by a local comedian, starting on the main civic square and taking in grave-robbing, a hilltop Victorian cemetery and a reputedly haunted hotel, finishing at one of the city’s oldest pubs near the river.

storyTitle.en-US: Stroll Through Time: A Walking Tour of Glasgow’s West End

storyDescription.en-US: A history of the university district and its scientists, alumni and music venues, starting at a station on the small orange underground, passing the Gothic university cloisters and a grand red sandstone museum, ending in a pub inside a converted church.

foodDescription.en-US: Rice toasted in butter with onion and beef marrow, cooked slowly in stock and turned deep gold with saffron, then finished with butter and Parmigiano. A popular legend credits a glassworker at the Duomo in 1574. Order it with ossobuco.

A thick cross-cut of veal shank braised slowly in white wine and stock until the meat comes off the bone, topped with gremolata: chopped lemon zest, garlic and parsley. The marrow in the middle is the prize, and some places bring a small spoon for it.

A veal chop on the bone, dipped in egg and breadcrumbs and fried in clarified butter. Milan and Vienna argue over who came first, this or the Wiener Schnitzel. The version beaten out to the size of the plate is called orecchia d’elefant, elephant’s ear.

Pork ribs, rind, trotters and small sausages stewed with Savoy cabbage, best after the first frost. A winter dish, traditionally started around 17 January, the feast of St Anthony the Abbot. Served with polenta, followed by a long walk.

Tripe cut into fine strips and simmered with white beans, carrot, celery and tomato, then finished with Parmigiano. Once the meal after midnight mass on Christmas Eve. Other Italians used to call the Milanese busecconi, tripe eaters, and it stuck.

Flattened meatballs of leftover boiled meat, mortadella or salami, milk-soaked bread and Parmigiano, fried in butter. The name is traced to the Spanish albóndiga. Thrift food turned bar food: look for them on aperitivo counters around six.

Tendons and cartilage from calves’ knees, boiled for hours, pressed, sliced thin and dressed with raw onion, oil and vinegar, sometimes with beans. Cold, chewy and translucent. A fixture of old osterie, where it is listed in dialect as gnervitt.

A thick soup of beans, cabbage, courgette, potato and whatever else is in season, made in Milan with rice rather than pasta and often a piece of pork rind for depth. In summer it is served at room temperature, which is how many locals prefer it.

A puffed white roll stamped with a star pattern, almost entirely crust and air, descended from the Austrian Kaisersemmel brought in under Habsburg rule. Good ones are getting rarer. Split one and fill it with mortadella, or with a slab of cotoletta.

A tall domed loaf of butter, eggs, candied orange and raisins, raised over days from a natural starter. Legend credits a kitchen boy named Toni at the Sforza court: pan de Toni. Keep a slice for 3 February, San Biagio’s day, said to protect the throat.

Sweet cornmeal buns scented with dried elderflower and dusted with sugar. Made for 23 April, the feast of St George, patron of Milan’s dairymen, and once eaten dipped in fresh cream. The name means millet bread, after the flour it was first made with.

Hot chocolate and coffee whipped with milk into a froth, drunk hot in winter and cold in summer. Named after Domenico Barbaja, a Milanese café waiter who became the great opera impresario of the 1800s, running La Scala and the San Carlo in Naples.

The bright red bitter that Gaspare Campari created in 1860 and his family went on to make in Milan. His son Davide opened the Camparino bar in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II arcade in 1915. Order a Campari Seltz at the counter there, standing up.

Campari and red vermouth topped with sparkling wine instead of gin. The story goes that Mirko Stocchetto, owner of Bar Basso, picked up the wrong bottle in the early 1970s. The bar still serves it, in an outsized goblet. Sbagliato means mistaken.

A half-moon of dough filled with tomato and mozzarella and fried until it puffs. Puglian by origin, made a Milanese habit by Luini, the bakery just off the Duomo square since 1949. The queue moves fast. Eat it on the pavement and mind the molten middle.

Round dumplings of grated raw and boiled potato, often stuffed with minced meat, served under fried onion and pork crackling. A Praga dish: women once sold them hot from jars at Bazar Różyckiego, the old east-bank market. Heavy, so plan a walk after.

Pork loin beaten thin, breaded and fried in lard until the edges curl, served with boiled potatoes and dill and a side of cabbage or cucumber salad. The Polish Sunday lunch. Milk bars do a cheap and honest one; the plate rarely leaves room for dessert.

Thin beef slices rolled around pickled cucumber, bacon and onion, tied with string and braised soft in dark gravy. Served with buckwheat groats or mashed potato. Old-school Warsaw restaurants keep them on the menu. Check for the string before you bite.

Cabbage leaves wrapped around minced pork and rice, baked or simmered and served under tomato or mushroom sauce. The name means little pigeons, and nobody can say why. A milk-bar staple and a home-cooking test: the leaf should cut with a fork.

Tomato soup made on the stock left from Sunday’s chicken broth, with rice or thin noodles and a swirl of sour cream. The Monday soup of every Polish household and every milk bar. Sweeter and creamier than a Spanish or Italian version, and cheap everywhere.

A cold summer soup of young beetroot and its leaves stirred into kefir or soured milk with cucumber, radish and dill, usually topped with half a boiled egg. Shocking pink and sharp. Only on menus in hot months, so order it when you see it.

Grated potato and onion fried in thin, crisp-edged pancakes. Eaten with sour cream or sugar, or folded around goulash as placek po węgiersku, Hungarian-style. A milk-bar classic; the ones fried to order beat the ones sitting under the lamp.

Thin pancakes folded around sweetened curd cheese, jam or fruit, sometimes fried again in butter and topped with cream. A cheap lunch rather than a dessert in milk bars like Prasowy on Marszałkowska Street. Savoury versions come with spinach or mushrooms.

Salted herring in oil with raw onion, or in sour cream with apple, eaten as a zakąska, a bite between shots of vodka. Warsaw’s late-night bars serve it for a few złoty a plate, the Polish currency. One shot, one bite is the rhythm.

Raw chopped beef with a raw egg yolk on top, surrounded by diced pickles, onion and pickled mushrooms that you mix in yourself. A starter in old restaurants and a vodka snack in all-night bars. The yolk may come in its half-shell so you can add it slowly.

Chocolate sponge soaked in punch, layered with thick whipped cream and covered in chocolate glaze. Created in Warsaw around 1950, most likely named after the W-Z route, the postwar east–west road through the rebuilt centre. Eat it with a fork, carefully.

Squares of soft vanilla mousse coated in chocolate, invented by Warsaw chocolatier Jan Wedel in 1936. The name is from the saying that a rich man has everything but bird’s milk. Sold in every corner shop; the vanilla box is the original.

Melted chocolate rather than cocoa, thick enough to stand a spoon in, served in Wedel’s chocolate lounges, the oldest on Szpitalna Street in the city centre. Order it plain or with chilli and expect to finish with a spoon. A glass of water helps.

A pink-and-white chewy sugar sweet, made in Praga since the 19th century. Sold from stalls outside Warsaw cemeteries such as Powązki on All Saints’ Day, 1 November. It sticks to your teeth; that is the point.

Fruit simmered in water with a little sugar and served cold in a glass, often with the fruit still in it: strawberries in summer, apples and plums in autumn. The default drink with a milk-bar lunch. Home versions vary wildly in sweetness.

Bacon, sausage, egg and black pudding, but what makes it Ulster is the bread: a soda farl and a slice of potato bread, both fried in the pan fat until golden. Beans are a point of dispute. Eaten late morning, followed by nothing until dinner.

Soda bread dough patted into a round, cut in four and cooked on a dry griddle rather than baked, so it comes out flat, floury and soft inside. Farl is from an old word for a quarter. Split it, fry it, and fill it with bacon or an egg.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin and cut into triangles, then browned on a griddle. Also called fadge or tattie bread. Unlike boxty it uses cooked potato only. Fried in butter it goes crisp and chewy at the same time.

Mashed potato beaten with hot milk and chopped scallions, piled up with a well of butter melting in the middle. Not colcannon, which has cabbage or kale; Ulster cooks will explain the difference unasked. Served beside sausages or boiled ham.

A big, round, soft white roll dusted in flour, with a dark crust on top that looks close to burnt. Bakeries pile them in the window. Split one for a bacon or sausage bap, or for a pastie bap, which is exactly what it sounds like.

A pastie here is no Cornish pasty: it is a round patty of minced pork, onion and potato, battered and deep-fried. Supper means it comes with chips. A Belfast chip shop order that needs salt, vinegar and nothing more complicated.

A ring doughnut, fried and rolled in sugar, under the name every Northern Irish bakery uses. Plain dough, no filling, no icing. Best still warm from the fryer, with a cup of tea, and a napkin for the sugar that will end up down your front.

A no-bake traybake of fifteen crushed digestive biscuits, fifteen marshmallows and fifteen glacé cherries, bound with condensed milk and rolled in coconut. Chilled and sliced. Sold in every café cabinet and nobody has ever needed a recipe card for it.

A domed bun between bread and sponge cake, with a crackled sugar top and sometimes a cherry or a few currants. Despite the name it has nothing to do with France. A Belfast bakery staple, cut in half and buttered by those who think it needs it.

Hard, golden honeycomb toffee made with golden syrup and baking soda, broken off the block with a hammer. Sold most famously at the Ould Lammas Fair in Ballycastle each August. Gets into your teeth and stays there; that is part of the deal.

Red seaweed gathered off the north Antrim coast and dried until leathery, then eaten straight from the bag as a salty snack. Traditionally paired with yellowman at the Lammas Fair. Look for it at St George’s Market. The taste is the sea, concentrated.

The first new potatoes of the year, grown in the light soil around Comber in County Down and with protected-name status since 2012. Thin-skinned and waxy, in shops from early summer. Boil them, add butter and salt, and that is the whole recipe.

Irish whiskey from the Old Bushmills Distillery on the north Antrim coast, which points to a 1608 royal licence to distil in the area. Triple-distilled and smooth. Ask for it neat or with a drop of water; Belfast bars stock several ages of it.

Northern Ireland’s own Tayto, made since 1956 at Tandragee Castle in County Armagh and unrelated to the Tayto brand in the Republic. Cheese and onion is the flagship flavour. A crisp sandwich in buttered white bread is a respected local lunch.

A dark, sticky malted loaf that has almost disappeared everywhere except Northern Ireland. Sold sliced in supermarkets, it is eaten toasted with plenty of butter and often a slice of cheese. Slightly sweet, slightly bitter, and best toasted.

Lamb or beef stewed for hours with potatoes, onions and carrots until the potatoes break down and thicken it. Named after lobscouse, a sailors’ stew, and the source of the city’s nickname. Eat it with pickled red cabbage or beetroot and buttered bread.

Scouse with no meat in it, made at the end of the week or the end of the money from potatoes, onions, carrots and stock. Still cooked at home and in some cafés. Thinner than the real thing and not pretending otherwise; the pickled cabbage does the work.

A dense slab of bread pudding or leftover cake, packed with dried fruit and soaked in syrup until it sags. The name is usually traced to Lord Nelson, via a richer Nelson cake. Heavy, sticky and cheap, a bakery staple. Eat it warm, with custard if offered.

Hard butter toffee first sold in the 1700s by Molly Bushell in Everton, then a village above the docks. It gave Everton FC its nickname, the Toffees, and before home games a Toffee Lady still throws Everton mints, striped boiled sweets, into the crowd.

A shortcrust tart filled with a whole lemon, peel and all, cooked down with brown sugar, butter and egg. Sharper and darker than a French lemon tart, with a faint bitterness from the rind. An old home recipe, now mostly found in cookbooks and the odd café.

Chips fried crisp, then tossed in a wok with salt, chilli, onion, peppers and five-spice. Liverpool’s Chinese takeaways claim them, and the city has Europe’s oldest Chinese community, so the claim holds up. Eat them fast, before the steam turns them soft.

Steamed dumplings, char siu pork buns and egg tarts in the restaurants around Nelson Street in Chinatown, under its ceremonial arch. The community dates to the 1860s, when the Blue Funnel shipping line began sailing to China. Go at weekend lunchtime.

The Friday tea from the chip shop: fish or a pie, chips, mushy peas and, here, curry sauce or gravy over the top. Many chippies here are Chinese-run, so the curry sauce is the takeaway kind. A chip butty, chips in a buttered roll, is the cheap option.

Minced beef, onion and potato in shortcrust, the matchday lunch around the football grounds. The best known come from Homebaked, the co-operative bakery on Oakfield Road opposite Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium. On match days they sell out before kick-off.

The two old Liverpool beers. Higsons bitter was the city’s pint for generations until the brewery closed in 1990; the name has since been revived. Cains brewed at the red-brick brewery on Stanhope Street. Try one in a Victorian pub like the Philharmonic.

Plain, dry, flaky crackers made by Jacob’s at its Aintree factory, north of the city, since 1914, near the racecourse where the Grand National is run. Eaten with butter and cheese. Trying to eat several without a drink is an old playground challenge.

Tiny brown shrimps from the sands off Southport, a seaside town north of the city, packed into pots under butter spiced with mace and nutmeg. Spread on hot toast so the butter melts. A Victorian seaside treat, still at fishmongers and on older menus.

White bread, butter and strawberry jam, folded or cut in half; a butty is any sandwich here. Comedian Ken Dodd, from the Knotty Ash district, spent a career joking about the jam butty mines worked by his Diddy Men. Best with a mug of tea.

Asparagus grown in the sandy coastal soil at Formby, north of Liverpool, a market-garden crop there for over a century. The season is short, roughly May and June. Eat it simply, with butter or a soft egg, and buy it from farm stands while it lasts.

Hard, flat ginger biscuits sold at the market in Ormskirk, a Lancashire market town just north of the city, where they have been made since the 1700s. Sold by the bag. They snap rather than bend and are best dunked in tea, the ginger arriving slowly.

Grilled chicken tikka in a creamy, mildly spiced tomato sauce. Glasgow’s claim: in the early 1970s Ali Ahmed Aslam at the Shish Mahal restaurant improvised the sauce, tomato soup included, for a diner who found his chicken dry. London disputes it.

A pizza box filled with whatever the takeaway has: doner meat, chicken pakora, chips, onion rings, garlic bread, naan, salad and several sauces, all piled together. Bought late at night from Glasgow’s Indian and Pakistani takeaways, and meant for sharing.

A cheese and tomato pizza, usually halved, dipped in fish batter and deep-fried until the crust crackles and the cheese runs. A Glasgow chip shop staple, ordered as a supper with chips. Eat it standing up, quickly, while the batter is still crisp.

Haggis, the peppery Scottish pudding of sheep’s offal and oats, broken into pieces, dipped in spiced chickpea batter and fried. A Glasgow curry-house starter that joins the city’s two food traditions. Served with a sweet red chilli dip or mint yogurt.

A Glasgow morning roll, floury and soft with a crust that shatters, split and filled with a slice of square sausage, also called Lorne. The local hangover breakfast. Add a fried egg or tattie scone, and choose red sauce or brown — people do care.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin, cut into triangles and cooked dry on a griddle. Fried again in the pan for a Scottish breakfast, or folded into a roll with square sausage. Supermarkets sell them in packs; bakeries’ are better.

Macaroni cheese baked inside a hot-water pastry case, sometimes browned on top under extra cheddar. Carbohydrate inside carbohydrate, sold warm in Glasgow bakeries and at football grounds. Locals eat them cold too, straight from the paper bag.

A Scotch pie of spiced mutton or beef, eaten with a cup of Bovril — a hot, salty beef-extract drink — at half time on the terraces. The standard winter ritual at Celtic Park, Ibrox and Hampden. Hold the pie upright or the grease goes everywhere.

Haddock, not cod, in batter with chips, wrapped and eaten hot. In Glasgow a supper means it comes with chips; a single fish means without. Many of the city’s chip shops were opened by Italian immigrant families, and some still are. Salt and vinegar on top.

Minced beef stewed slowly with onion and carrot until it turns into thick gravy, served with plain boiled or mashed potatoes. The everyday Glasgow dinner for generations. Unglamorous, comforting, and still on the menu in old-fashioned cafés.

A spiced fruit pudding of flour, suet, dried fruit and treacle, wrapped in a cloth — a cloot — and boiled for hours until it forms a dark, shiny skin. Sliced and eaten with custard, or fried for breakfast the next morning. Made at Christmas and birthdays.

A round shortbread biscuit topped with a dome of soft white marshmallow and coated in thin milk chocolate, in red and silver foil. Made by Tunnock’s in Uddingston, east of the city, since 1956. Giant dancing versions opened the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Glasgow’s word for an ice cream cone, sold from ice cream vans and from the cafés opened by Italian families who arrived from the late 1800s. Vanilla is standard. Ask for a ninety-nine and you get a chocolate flake pushed in the top.

A bright orange fizzy drink made by AG Barr, a Glasgow firm, since 1901, now produced in Cumbernauld. Sweet, faintly of bubblegum and citrus, with a secret recipe. Scots drink it as a hangover cure. A Glaswegian may call any fizzy drink ginger.

A pale, crisp lager brewed at the Wellpark Brewery in the city’s East End, beside the Necropolis cemetery, where Tennent’s began making lager in 1885. The default pint in almost every Glasgow pub. Ask for a pint of Tennent’s and nobody will ask which size.

context.en-US: Still buongiorno until mid-afternoon. Buon pomeriggio exists but is rarely said to strangers.

groupNote.en-US: Buonasera starts in the afternoon, from about four. Milanese often clip both to ’giorno and ’sera.

context.en-US: Hello and goodbye, for friends and peers. Among friends you will also hear Uè (weh), a loud all-purpose Milanese hey.
Buona giornata (have a good day) on the way out is just as common, and Milanese shopkeepers will say it first.
Three syllables, not two. Grazie mille is a thousand thanks.
Often answered in English before you finish. Milan does business in it.
For a real apology. For a bump on the metro, scusi is the word.
Say it on a packed tram or metro before you move toward the doors.
Milan eats dinner around eight, earlier than Rome. Book on Fridays and Saturdays.
If you’re warm and kind, this is enough to get by. More polite version: Il menù, per favore.
The clink at aperitivo. Salute (sah-LOO-teh) is the plainer toast, and also what you say after a sneeze.
More polite version: Il conto, per favore. At a busy coffee bar, pay first at the till and hand the receipt to the barista.
A per-person charge for bread and the table, printed on the menu. Legitimate. At aperitivo the drink price usually includes the snacks.
On the metro you can tap a contactless bank card at the gates instead of buying one. Keep it to tap out.
Bars expect you to buy something first. A coffee at the counter is the usual price of entry.

groupNote.en-US: Also Signori (men) and Signore (women), one vowel apart on adjacent doors.

context.en-US: Not to be confused with ATM, the city’s transport company, whose logo is on every tram stop. Decline the offer to charge you in dollars.
Cards are accepted almost everywhere, including for a single espresso.
Worth a few coins for market stalls, newsstands and the odd old bar.
Charged by law. Say no grazie if you brought one.
Dialect for signora: the well-dressed, well-off older Milanese lady, fur coat in winter, small dog, firm opinions, coffee at the same bar every day. Said with affection, and some caution.
A braggart, roughly one who drools while boasting. AC Milan fans use it for Inter fans, and Inter fans have adopted it with pride. The two clubs share San Siro stadium.
“Milan to drink”: a 1980s advertising slogan for Ramazzotti, a Milanese herbal liqueur, that became the name for the city’s high-living decade, and for the bribery scandals that ended it.
Aperitivo plus cena, dinner: an early-evening drink with a buffet substantial enough to replace the meal. The bars along the Navigli canals are where it is taken most seriously.
Dialect for “I’ll take care of it.” The Milanese motto of quiet self-reliance and getting on with the job, quoted with pride and, increasingly, with irony.
The same phrase all day: literally “good day.” Polish has no separate afternoon greeting.

groupNote.en-US: The switch comes when it gets dark, so as early as four in a Warsaw winter.

context.en-US: Hello and goodbye both, for friends and people your age. Hej (hey) is softer and common among younger Varsovians.
Literally “until seeing.” Say it on the way out of a shop even if you bought nothing.
Also “you’re welcome,” “here you go” and, on the phone, “go ahead.” Poproszę (poh-PROH-sheh) means “I’ll have” when ordering.
Dzięki (JEN-kee) is the casual version.
You’ll hear no (noh) constantly. It means “yeah” or “well,” not no.

title.en-US: Warsaw · Czy mówi pan po angielsku?

context.en-US: Pan to a man, pani (PAH-nee) to a woman. Most young Varsovians speak English well, so a plain hello first is enough.
The same word apologises, gets attention and clears a path.
On a packed tram, ask Wysiada pan? (vi-SHAH-dah pahn): are you getting off? If not, they let you through.

groupNote.en-US: One word for all three. Polish doesn’t split them.

context.en-US: Literally “a little table for two people.” In milk bars you order at the counter and sit anywhere.
If you’re warm and kind, this is enough to get by. More polite version: Poproszę menu.
Point as you say it. Also works at bakery counters and market stalls.
Said by waiters, by people at the next table, and to you by anyone who walks in while you eat.
Look people in the eye. With vodka, follow the shot with a bite of food straight away.
If you’re warm and kind, this is enough to get by. More polite version: Poproszę rachunek. To tip by card, say the amount before the waiter keys it in.
Since October 2025 bottles and cans carry a deposit, 50 groszy for plastic and cans, added at the till. Return them to larger shops to get it back.
One ticket covers trams, buses, metro and city trains. Validate a paper ticket in the small yellow box when you first board. Inspectors are common.
WC on signs. Station and park toilets often charge a couple of złoty.

groupNote.en-US: Often no words at all: a triangle means men, a circle means women.

context.en-US: Use bank-branded machines rather than the standalone ones near the Old Town. Decline the offer to charge you in dollars or pounds.
Ile? alone does the job at a market stall.
Say it as you hold the card up. Contactless and phone payment are universal, even at bazaar stalls.
Poland isn’t in the euro. Prices are in złoty (ZWOH-ti), and euros get a poor rate where they’re taken at all.
Charged at the till. Say nie, dziękuję if you brought one.
The city’s nickname for itself, on T-shirts, in rap lyrics and in text messages. Affectionate when locals say it, slightly cheeky from anyone else.
Beijing: locals’ nickname for the Palace of Culture and Science, from its initials PKiN. Stalin’s gift to the city, and the old joke says the best view is from the top, where you can’t see it.
A jar: the half-joking word for newcomers from the provinces who go home at weekends and come back with jars of their mother’s cooking. Most of Warsaw’s workforce, by that measure.
W-hour: 5pm on 1 August, when the Warsaw Uprising against the German occupation began in 1944. Sirens sound every year, and traffic and pedestrians stop where they are for a minute.
The little mermaid with sword and shield on Warsaw’s coat of arms. Her statue stands in the Old Town Market Square and another on the Vistula bank. Also the name of a communist-era car.
Universal across Northern Ireland, from bus drivers to bank managers.
Not at all is the standard reply to thanks, and means you’re welcome rather than no.
The usual thanks at a bar or counter. Thanks very much is the fuller form.
A greeting, not a question, usually squashed to ’bout ye. “Not bad, yourself?” closes it.
Still current here. Bye is often said several times in a row on the way out the door.
The same reflex as Britain. Also means “pardon?”
Bar service runs on eye contact and patience. The bar staff know who came in when.

groupNote.en-US: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

context.en-US: Can I get passes here without comment. A wee one of anything is also understood.
Class works among younger people: that was class means excellent.
Asking for the check marks you instantly.
Less common than in London and usually only for big groups. Check the bill before you tip around 10%.
Translink Metro buses and the Glider take contactless. On the Glider you pay at the stop, not on board.
Loo works. The bogs is cruder and common. Restroom gets a blank look.
Northern Irish banks print their own sterling notes. They’re valid across the UK but shops in England sometimes refuse them.
Contactless everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Still useful at St George’s Market stalls and in older pubs.
Charged since 2013. Say no thanks if you brought one.
Small, and also a softener attached to almost anything. A wee cup of tea, a wee minute, a wee drive to Bangor, which is not that wee.
Fine, sound, agreed. He’s dead on is a compliment; dead on, see you at eight settles a plan. Dead on its own just means very.
Get a grip, don’t be ridiculous. Said to someone talking nonsense, usually with a laugh, sometimes without one.
Mortified, deeply embarrassed. The feeling of waving back at someone who was waving at the person behind you.
Northern Ireland, said fast in a Belfast accent and written down as a joke. Mostly heard from football fans and on the terraces at Windsor Park stadium.
The all-purpose agreement: fine, good, that works. Said of a person, he’s sound is real praise.
Used with strangers as well as friends, and not considered sloppy. Cheers works just as well.
A greeting, not a question. “Sound, you?” closes it. Men add la (lad) and women often get queen or girl, all of it friendly.
The local goodbye, often stretched to ta-ra well. See you later works too.
The same reflex as the rest of England. Also means “what did you say?”, which you may need for the accent.
At a bar, stand where the staff can see you and wait your turn. Waving money or calling out gets you served later.

groupNote.en-US: Sorry works for apologising and for getting past. Excuse me is for asking something.

context.en-US: Some British people hear “Can I get” as too American. Liverpool barely notices; “Can I have” is the safe version.
That was boss covers food, a night out or a goal. Nothing to do with anyone’s employer.
Ask for the check and you’ll be understood, and marked as American.
Some restaurants add 10–12.5% to the bill. It should be printed on the bill and can be removed if you ask, so check before tipping on top.
Loo works, and bogs is cruder but common. Ask for the restroom and you’ll get a blank look.

groupNote.en-US: Standard on most doors. Pubs occasionally get creative with the signs.

context.en-US: Local buses take a tapped bank card or phone. Merseyrail, the local train network that loops under the city centre, needs a ticket from a machine or app before you board.
Also the hole in the wall. Bank-branded machines are free; some in shops and pubs charge a fee.
Contactless almost everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Still handy in older pubs, chippies and at the match, though card works nearly everywhere.

title.en-US: Liverpool · Do you want a bag?

context.en-US: The cashier is asking if you want a bag, which costs extra. Say no thanks if you brought one.

meaning.en-US: Lad, used to address a man, friend or stranger: alright, la? Lid is the older version. Not rude in any way.
Delighted. I’m made up for you means you’re genuinely pleased for them. Nothing to do with lying or make-up.
Fake or counterfeit, as in a jarg watch or a jarg football shirt. Also a person who isn’t what they claim to be.
Food. Sailors used the word long before Liverpool did, and the port kept it. Is there any scran? means what’s to eat.
A protest at something unfair, said in a rising whine: ar eh, give us a go. Close to “oh, come on.”

context.en-US: Universal, at every age and in every setting. Aye, right — with the stress on right — means the opposite.
Also nae for “not” — nae bother means no problem.
A greeting, not a question. “No bad, yersel?” closes it. Awright? does the same job in one word.
Cheerio is still current. Shop staff often send you off with cheers, pal or cheers, hen — pal for men, hen for women.
Standard. Thanks very much is fine; ta is understood but sounds English.
Used freely. Sorry? also means “what did you say,” which you may need often.
Bar staff work out the order from who arrived when. A nod and eye contact are enough; waving money is not.

groupNote.en-US: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

context.en-US: Or just name it — a pint of Tennent’s, please. Glasgow is not fussy about phrasing.
Asking for the check marks you instantly, though nobody will mind.
Sometimes added for groups and shown at the bottom of the bill. Otherwise tipping around 10% for table service is normal.
Tap a bank card on most city buses. The Subway is a single circular line, nicknamed the Clockwork Orange after its trains.
Loo works and the cludgie is old Glasgow slang for it. Restroom gets a blank look.

groupNote.en-US: Standard on most doors. Gaelic signs at stations use Fir for men and Mnathan for women.

context.en-US: Also the hole in the wall. Cash machines here dispense Scottish banknotes.
Contactless almost everywhere, including most chip shops and taxis.
Three Scottish banks print their own notes. They are legal across the UK but some English shops hesitate, so spend them here.
Charged. Doing the messages means doing the grocery shopping, so bring one if you are.
Glasgow’s favourite compliment for a person or a move with some swagger. Originally it meant fit for the gallows.
From wee ane, little one. The weans are the kids, and a greetin’ wean is a crying one.
Irn-Bru, cola, lemonade — all ginger in Glasgow. A bottle of ginger has nothing to do with ginger.
For a smell, a room, a pub toilet or the weather. Also used of a person who badly needs a wash.
One of many Glasgow words for it, alongside blootered and mortal. Usually said with some admiration.
